### Findings

**should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh:55`: the private server still loads the developer's `~/.tmux.conf`, so a common user setting turns the test red and blames the game.**

`tm() { tmux -L "$socket" "$@"; }` gives a private *socket* but not a private *config*. `set -g base-index 1` / `set -g pane-base-index 1` — one of the most widespread tmux customisations — moves the pane away from the hard-coded `pane="tui:0.0"`, every `capture-pane` fails into `2>/dev/null`, and `screen()` returns nothing. Reproduced against the current staged script:

```
$ HOME=<home with base-index 1> ./tests/tui.sh <sst>
FAIL: 80x24: the game never asked its first question
  --- screen ---
(empty)
```

That message names a game defect that does not exist, and the empty dump gives no clue where to look. Same exposure, lower probability, for `default-terminal` (would trip the new `" Status "` panel assertion via a `tui_init()` fallback) and `default-shell` (the command string is handed to it). CI is unaffected — the runners have no `~/.tmux.conf` — so this only ever bites a human, which is the worst place for it.

Fix (verified: with the same hostile `HOME` the script goes from the failure above to `tui OK`):

```sh
tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }
```

Worth mirroring in the hand-driving recipe in `AGENTS.md:50` so an agent following it by hand gets the same isolation.

**nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:16`: the comment claims slightly more than the flag knows.**

`typed = TRUE` is set at the top of `readinput()`, before the read returns, so the flag really means "the game has asked the player for a line" — on the EOF path it is set although nothing was typed. Behaviourally identical (nothing prints during the read) and the placement is the right one, but "The player has typed something at least once" is a shade stronger than the code. "The game has asked the player for a line at least once" would state it exactly, and the `skip()` comment reads correctly as-is either way.

**nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:743`: the `skip()` comment argues entirely in `-t` terms for a gate that also governs plain mode.**

It is a no-op there today only because `scan()` resets `linecount` often enough that the 23-line threshold is never reached before the first prompt. A half-sentence saying the gate is deliberately mode-independent, and that plain mode is unaffected only because nothing before the first `scan()` reaches 23 lines, would stop a future preamble change from silently altering plain output.

### Notes on the test additions (no action needed)

The argv case and the two polling loops are the right additions and are not vacuous: the "manual stopped paging after its first screen" loop watches for 4 s rather than sampling once, `to_command()` only sends Space while a pause prompt is actually on screen, and `unwanted "UNRECOGNIZED"` matches a string that really exists (`sst.c:245,247`). The `" Status "`/`" Quadrant "` assertions do distinguish curses from the fallback — I confirmed the strings only appear as panel borders. The one remaining fixed sleep (line 180, before sending the password) is safe: keystrokes sent early sit in the tty input queue until `wgetnstr()` asks, and any real failure surfaces at the following `to_command()`.

### Not reviewed

- macOS CI: I could not exercise `runner.os == 'macOS'` — whether `tmux-256color` resolves for the game there, and whether `brew list tmux` short-circuits on the image, will only be answered by the first PR run. The Linux job I effectively reproduced locally.

CI is unaffected — the runners have no `~/.tmux.conf` — so this only ever bites a human, which is the worst place for it.

Fix (verified: with the same hostile `HOME` the script goes from the failure above to `tui OK`):

```sh
tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }
```

Worth mirroring in the hand-driving recipe in `AGENTS.md:50` so an agent following it by hand gets the same isolation.

`typed = TRUE` is set at the top of `readinput()`, before the read returns, so the flag really means "the game has asked the player for a line" — on the EOF path it is set although nothing was typed. Behaviourally identical (nothing prints during the read) and the placement is the right one, but "The player has typed something at least once" is a shade stronger than the code. "The game has asked the player for a line at least once" would state it exactly, and the `skip()` comment reads correctly as-is either way.

**nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:743`: the `skip()` comment argues entirely in `-t` terms for a gate that also governs plain mode.**

It is a no-op there today only because `scan()` resets `linecount` often enough that the 23-line threshold is never reached before the first prompt. A half-sentence saying the gate is deliberately mode-independent, and that plain mode is unaffected only because nothing before the first `scan()` reaches 23 lines, would stop a future preamble change from silently altering plain output.

### Notes on the test additions (no action needed)

The argv case and the two polling loops are the right additions and are not vacuous: the "manual stopped paging after its first screen" loop watches for 4 s rather than sampling once, `to_command()` only sends Space while a pause prompt is actually on screen, and `unwanted "UNRECOGNIZED"` matches a string that really exists (`sst.c:245,247`). The `" Status "`/`" Quadrant "` assertions do distinguish curses from the fallback — I confirmed the strings only appear as panel borders. The one remaining fixed sleep (line 180, before sending the password) is safe: keystrokes sent early sit in the tty input queue until `wgetnstr()` asks, and any real failure surfaces at the following `to_command()`.

- macOS CI: I could not exercise `runner.os == 'macOS'` — whether `tmux-256color` resolves for the game there, and whether `brew list tmux` short-circuits on the image, will only be answered by the first PR run. The Linux job I effectively reproduced locally.

#!/bin/sh
# Drives the full-screen display through a real terminal.
#
# Everything else in the suite talks to the game through pipes, which
# is enough for the fallback path but never exercises curses itself.
# This one runs the game inside tmux so there is a genuine pty, and
# reads the screen back the way a player would see it.
#
# The size matters. 80x24 is what most terminal emulators open at and
# 72x24 is the smallest the TUI accepts; at both the message window is
# only ten lines, so the startup banner overflows it -- which is how
# the pager came to be waiting for a keystroke before the game had
# asked the player anything, and to eat the first letter of the answer.
#
# Usage: tui.sh /path/to/sst
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) when there is no tmux to run in.
#
# Needs a sleep that takes a fraction, which GNU and BSD both have but
# POSIX does not promise; busybox would need whole seconds.

set -u

SST="${1:-./sst}"
case "$SST" in
	/*) ;;
	*) SST="$(pwd)/$SST" ;;
esac
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)

if ! command -v tmux >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	# A developer without tmux gets a skip. CI does not: this is the
	# only test that runs curses at all, and a green build that quietly
	# skipped it would be worse than no test.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ]; then
		echo "FAIL: tmux is missing on CI, so the TUI went untested" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: tmux is not installed, so there is no pty to test in" >&2
	exit 77
fi
if [ ! -x "$SST" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $SST is not executable" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Run on a socket of our own, never the default one. A developer's tmux
# server is usually sitting on the default socket with a day's real work
# in it, and anything server-wide -- this script's cleanup, or an agent
# tidying up after driving the TUI by hand -- takes that down too. -L
# buys a private server, so cleanup can be as blunt as it needs to be.
socket="sst-tui-$$"
session="tui"
pane="$session:0.0"

tm() { tmux -L "$socket" "$@"; }

# tmux leaves the socket file behind when the server exits, so a suite
# that ran often would slowly fill the directory with dead ones. Where
# tmux puts them is a guess -- right on Linux, and on macOS the sockets
# go under $TMPDIR instead, where this quietly does nothing.
cleanup() {
	tm kill-server 2>/dev/null
	rm -f "${TMUX_TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-$(id -u)/$socket"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'cleanup; exit 130' INT
trap 'cleanup; exit 143' TERM
trap 'cleanup; exit 129' HUP

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

screen() { tm capture-pane -t "$pane" -p 2>/dev/null; }

dump() {
	printf '  --- screen ---\n' >&2
	screen | sed 's/^/  | /' >&2
}

# Wait until the screen shows $1, up to about eight seconds. Polling
# beats a fixed sleep: curses paints in its own time, and a machine
# under load should not turn into a failure.
wait_for() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 80 ]; do
		if screen | grep -qF "$1"; then return 0; fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.1
	done
	return 1
}

# Answer any paging prompts until the command prompt comes back. A
# space is only ever sent while a pause is actually showing, so this
# cannot quietly paper over a pause that should not have been there.
to_command() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
		screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND' && return 0
		if screen | grep -qE 'CONTINUE|HIT SPACE BAR'; then
			tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
		fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.25
	done
	return 1
}

want() {
	screen | grep -qF "$2" || { fail "$1"; dump; }
}

unwanted() {
	if screen | grep -qF "$2"; then fail "$1"; dump; fi
}

# tmux takes a shell command line, not an argument list, so the path
# has to survive being quoted into one.
sstq=$(printf "%s" "$SST" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g")

# Start the game on a terminal $1 wide by $2 tall, passing $3 (if any)
# on the command line. It reads sst.doc from the current directory, and
# dies with the session.
start() {
	cleanup
	tm new-session -d -x "$1" -y "$2" -s "$session" -c "$srcdir" \
		"'$sstq' -t ${3:-}; sleep 30" 2>/dev/null || {
		echo "FAIL: could not start a ${1}x${2} tmux session" >&2
		exit 1
	}
}

# --- the game asks before it pauses, at every size it accepts -------
# 80x24 is what most emulators open at; 72x24 is the smallest the TUI
# will run in. The banner is longer than the message window at both, so
# it scrolls -- ordinary. Stopping to ask for a keystroke is not:
# nothing has been asked yet, so there is no reader to wait for, and
# the prompt sits exactly where the player is about to type an answer.
for size in 80x24 72x24; do
	cols=${size%x*}
	rows=${size#*x}
	start "$cols" "$rows"

	if ! wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'; then
		fail "$size: the game never asked its first question"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	# Curses is really running, not the classic display falling back
	# inside the pty. Without this every assertion below is satisfied
	# by the plain path, and a broken tui_init() would still look
	# green -- from a script whose whole point is to exercise curses.
	# The panel titles are drawn in TUI mode and nowhere else.
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Status "
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Quadrant "

	unwanted "$size: paused with [HIT SPACE BAR] before asking anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	unwanted "$size: paused with [CONTINUE?] before asking anything" "[CONTINUE?]"

	# With a pager waiting, its getch() swallowed the leading
	# character and the game saw "egular".
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'regular' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Short, Medium, or Long'; then
		fail "$size: the game did not accept 'regular' as the first answer"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	unwanted "$size: the first answer lost a character" 'What is "'
done

# --- paging still works once the game is running --------------------
# Carrying on from the 72x24 game above: the rest of setup, then the
# briefing, which does page.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'short' Enter
wait_for 'Novice, Fair, Good, Expert' || fail "setup did not reach the skill question"
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'novice' Enter
sleep 0.5
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'xyz' Enter
if ! to_command; then
	fail "the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
	exit 1
fi

# A manual entry runs well past the ten-line message window, so it has
# to page -- the fix must only have quietened the pauses nobody asked
# for, not the ones that do the job.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'help move' Enter
if ! wait_for 'CONTINUE'; then
	fail "long output no longer pages"
	dump
fi
# And the pause really does hold: still there a moment later, waiting,
# rather than having flashed past on its own.
sleep 0.5
want "the paging prompt did not wait for a keystroke" "CONTINUE"

# One keystroke buys one screen, not the whole entry. A gate that
# switched paging off again after the first pause would let the rest of
# the manual scroll away, and answering pauses until the prompt returns
# would not notice: the manual runs to several screens, so the command
# prompt must not be back yet.
# Watched for a few seconds rather than sampled once: a single look
# after a fixed sleep passes on a machine that has not repainted yet.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 16 ]; do
	if screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND'; then
		fail "the manual stopped paging after its first screen"
		dump
		break
	fi
	i=$((i + 1))
	sleep 0.25
done

# Spaces get it moving again -- however many pages the entry runs to.
to_command || fail "the manual never finished paging"

# The game is still listening. Long-range scan says something the
# always-on panels never do, so this cannot pass on their text.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
	fail "the game did not carry on after the paging prompt"
	dump
fi

# --- setup answered on the command line ------------------------------
# The same bug reaches further than the banner. With the setup answers
# in argv the player never types during setup at all, so the game runs
# on into the briefing -- and a pause there waits for, and eats, the
# first character of their first command.
#
# The briefing's fixed text is already longer than the window, so the
# case does not rest on the galaxy that gets generated; the seed only
# decides how much further past the threshold it goes, and rand()
# differing between C libraries can blunt that but not invert it. A
# pause before the player has touched the keyboard is wrong either way.
start 80 24 'tournament 5 long emeritus xyz'
if ! wait_for 'COMMAND'; then
	fail "argv setup: the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
else
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "CONTINUE"
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	# Long-range scan rather than short: its heading appears only in
	# the message window, so waiting for it proves the command was
	# read whole. Sampling the screen after a fixed sleep instead
	# would pass on a slow machine that had not repainted yet.
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
		fail "argv setup: the first command was not accepted"
		dump
	fi
	unwanted "argv setup: the first command lost a character" "UNRECOGNIZED"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'tui OK\n'

# AGENTS.md

Shared instructions for every coding agent working in this repository
(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and others). `CLAUDE.md` imports this
file; keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing.

## Project

Super Star Trek — a classic terminal (CLI) space strategy game written in C17,
built with CMake. The executable is `sst`. Game documentation lives in
`sst.doc`; shared declarations live in `sst.h`.

Global game state uses the `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`: exactly one
translation unit per binary defines `INCLUDED` before including `sst.h` to
instantiate the globals (`sst.c` for the game; a test's own file, e.g.
`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, for test binaries that don't link `sst.c`).

## Build and run

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # build type is required; Debug adds -DDEBUG
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

Note: `CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so configuring
without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=...` fails. Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE
-DCLOAKING` are always enabled.

## TUI mode (`sst -t`)

- All game output must go through `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`prouts` and all
  input through `scan()`/`getch()`/`readinput()` — raw `printf`/`putchar`/
  `fgets` silently bypasses the full-screen mode.
- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
  and explain why.
- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
  filter that shape before checking.
- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
  sync (`ctest --test-dir build`).
- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
  `-L` — `tmux -L sst new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep
  30'`, drive with `tmux -L sst send-keys -t t 'cmd' Enter` (input is
  line-based; keys need Enter), inspect with `tmux -L sst capture-pane -t t -p`,
  and clean up with `tmux -L sst kill-server`. The default socket is where the
  human running you keeps their own work: on 2026-08-01 a review agent tidied up
  after a TUI check with a bare `tmux kill-server` and destroyed a week-old
  session of eight panes, including the agent's own parent. `-L` is what makes
  that mistake impossible rather than merely discouraged — never issue a bare
  `tmux kill-server`, and never `kill-session` a session you did not create.
  Never redirect the game's stdout in the session — it breaks curses rendering.
  `tests/tui.sh` does all of this automatically and is the place to add
  coverage; it skips without tmux, but fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is
  set.
- Check the TUI at 80x24 and 72x24, not just at a comfortable size. 72x24 is
  the smallest it accepts and 80x24 is what most terminals open at; the
  message window is only ten lines at both, which is where the paging bugs
  live.

## Development workflow

Every coding agent working in this repository must follow this workflow.

1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.

2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
   `main` state.

3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a roadmap item or
   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
   sub-agent must act as an expert in games and CLI games.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to
   run the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for
   the change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage,
   and environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
   rerun the verifier after addressing it.

8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for
   the changed state.

9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:

   ```text
   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**

#!/bin/sh
# Drives the full-screen display through a real terminal.
#
# Everything else in the suite talks to the game through pipes, which
# is enough for the fallback path but never exercises curses itself.
# This one runs the game inside tmux so there is a genuine pty, and
# reads the screen back the way a player would see it.
#
# The size matters. 80x24 is what most terminal emulators open at and
# 72x24 is the smallest the TUI accepts; at both the message window is
# only ten lines, so the startup banner overflows it -- which is how
# the pager came to be waiting for a keystroke before the game had
# asked the player anything, and to eat the first letter of the answer.
#
# Usage: tui.sh /path/to/sst
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) when there is no tmux to run in.
#
# Needs a sleep that takes a fraction, which GNU and BSD both have but
# POSIX does not promise; busybox would need whole seconds.

set -u

SST="${1:-./sst}"
case "$SST" in
	/*) ;;
	*) SST="$(pwd)/$SST" ;;
esac
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)

if ! command -v tmux >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	# A developer without tmux gets a skip. CI does not: this is the
	# only test that runs curses at all, and a green build that quietly
	# skipped it would be worse than no test.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ]; then
		echo "FAIL: tmux is missing on CI, so the TUI went untested" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: tmux is not installed, so there is no pty to test in" >&2
	exit 77
fi
if [ ! -x "$SST" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $SST is not executable" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Run on a socket of our own, never the default one. A developer's tmux
# server is usually sitting on the default socket with a day's real work
# in it, and anything server-wide -- this script's cleanup, or an agent
# tidying up after driving the TUI by hand -- takes that down too. -L
# buys a private server, so cleanup can be as blunt as it needs to be.
socket="sst-tui-$$"
session="tui"
pane="$session:0.0"

# -f /dev/null as well as -L: a private socket is not a private config,
# and `set -g base-index 1` -- one of the commoner things people put in
# ~/.tmux.conf -- moves the pane out from under the name used below, so
# every capture comes back empty and the game gets blamed for it.
tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }

# tmux leaves the socket file behind when the server exits, so a suite
# that ran often would slowly fill the directory with dead ones. Where
# tmux puts them is a guess -- right on Linux, and on macOS the sockets
# go under $TMPDIR instead, where this quietly does nothing.
cleanup() {
	tm kill-server 2>/dev/null
	rm -f "${TMUX_TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-$(id -u)/$socket"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'cleanup; exit 130' INT
trap 'cleanup; exit 143' TERM
trap 'cleanup; exit 129' HUP

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

screen() { tm capture-pane -t "$pane" -p 2>/dev/null; }

dump() {
	printf '  --- screen ---\n' >&2
	screen | sed 's/^/  | /' >&2
}

# Wait until the screen shows $1, up to about eight seconds. Polling
# beats a fixed sleep: curses paints in its own time, and a machine
# under load should not turn into a failure.
wait_for() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 80 ]; do
		if screen | grep -qF "$1"; then return 0; fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.1
	done
	return 1
}

# Answer any paging prompts until the command prompt comes back. A
# space is only ever sent while a pause is actually showing, so this
# cannot quietly paper over a pause that should not have been there.
to_command() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
		screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND' && return 0
		if screen | grep -qE 'CONTINUE|HIT SPACE BAR'; then
			tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
		fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.25
	done
	return 1
}

want() {
	screen | grep -qF "$2" || { fail "$1"; dump; }
}

unwanted() {
	if screen | grep -qF "$2"; then fail "$1"; dump; fi
}

# tmux takes a shell command line, not an argument list, so the path
# has to survive being quoted into one.
sstq=$(printf "%s" "$SST" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g")

# Start the game on a terminal $1 wide by $2 tall, passing $3 (if any)
# on the command line. It reads sst.doc from the current directory, and
# dies with the session.
start() {
	cleanup
	tm new-session -d -x "$1" -y "$2" -s "$session" -c "$srcdir" \
		"'$sstq' -t ${3:-}; sleep 30" 2>/dev/null || {
		echo "FAIL: could not start a ${1}x${2} tmux session" >&2
		exit 1
	}
}

# --- the game asks before it pauses, at every size it accepts -------
# 80x24 is what most emulators open at; 72x24 is the smallest the TUI
# will run in. The banner is longer than the message window at both, so
# it scrolls -- ordinary. Stopping to ask for a keystroke is not:
# nothing has been asked yet, so there is no reader to wait for, and
# the prompt sits exactly where the player is about to type an answer.
for size in 80x24 72x24; do
	cols=${size%x*}
	rows=${size#*x}
	start "$cols" "$rows"

	if ! wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'; then
		fail "$size: the game never asked its first question"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	# Curses is really running, not the classic display falling back
	# inside the pty. Without this every assertion below is satisfied
	# by the plain path, and a broken tui_init() would still look
	# green -- from a script whose whole point is to exercise curses.
	# The panel titles are drawn in TUI mode and nowhere else.
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Status "
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Quadrant "

	unwanted "$size: paused with [HIT SPACE BAR] before asking anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	unwanted "$size: paused with [CONTINUE?] before asking anything" "[CONTINUE?]"

	# With a pager waiting, its getch() swallowed the leading
	# character and the game saw "egular".
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'regular' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Short, Medium, or Long'; then
		fail "$size: the game did not accept 'regular' as the first answer"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	unwanted "$size: the first answer lost a character" 'What is "'
done

# --- paging still works once the game is running --------------------
# Carrying on from the 72x24 game above: the rest of setup, then the
# briefing, which does page.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'short' Enter
wait_for 'Novice, Fair, Good, Expert' || fail "setup did not reach the skill question"
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'novice' Enter
sleep 0.5
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'xyz' Enter
if ! to_command; then
	fail "the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
	exit 1
fi

# A manual entry runs well past the ten-line message window, so it has
# to page -- the fix must only have quietened the pauses nobody asked
# for, not the ones that do the job.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'help move' Enter
if ! wait_for 'CONTINUE'; then
	fail "long output no longer pages"
	dump
fi
# And the pause really does hold: still there a moment later, waiting,
# rather than having flashed past on its own.
sleep 0.5
want "the paging prompt did not wait for a keystroke" "CONTINUE"

# One keystroke buys one screen, not the whole entry. A gate that
# switched paging off again after the first pause would let the rest of
# the manual scroll away, and answering pauses until the prompt returns
# would not notice: the manual runs to several screens, so the command
# prompt must not be back yet.
# Watched for a few seconds rather than sampled once: a single look
# after a fixed sleep passes on a machine that has not repainted yet.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 16 ]; do
	if screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND'; then
		fail "the manual stopped paging after its first screen"
		dump
		break
	fi
	i=$((i + 1))
	sleep 0.25
done

# Spaces get it moving again -- however many pages the entry runs to.
to_command || fail "the manual never finished paging"

# The game is still listening. Long-range scan says something the
# always-on panels never do, so this cannot pass on their text.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
	fail "the game did not carry on after the paging prompt"
	dump
fi

# --- setup answered on the command line ------------------------------
# The same bug reaches further than the banner. With the setup answers
# in argv the player never types during setup at all, so the game runs
# on into the briefing -- and a pause there waits for, and eats, the
# first character of their first command.
#
# The briefing's fixed text is already longer than the window, so the
# case does not rest on the galaxy that gets generated; the seed only
# decides how much further past the threshold it goes, and rand()
# differing between C libraries can blunt that but not invert it. A
# pause before the player has touched the keyboard is wrong either way.
start 80 24 'tournament 5 long emeritus xyz'
if ! wait_for 'COMMAND'; then
	fail "argv setup: the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
else
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "CONTINUE"
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	# Long-range scan rather than short: its heading appears only in
	# the message window, so waiting for it proves the command was
	# read whole. Sampling the screen after a fixed sleep instead
	# would pass on a slow machine that had not repainted yet.
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
		fail "argv setup: the first command was not accepted"
		dump
	fi
	unwanted "argv setup: the first command lost a character" "UNRECOGNIZED"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'tui OK\n'

Everything for **#17 is done and code-review approved** — but 1Password's SSH agent has dropped again, so the commit can't be signed (two attempts, `Could not connect to socket specified by SSH_AUTH_SOCK`). All five files are staged.

**What the fix turned out to be.** The gate belongs in `readinput()`, not `scan()` — and that distinction was the whole review. My first cut set the flag in `scan()`, reasoning that argv-supplied setup answers never reach `readinput()`. Code review showed that argument was backwards: because argv answers are chewed from a prefilled buffer, a gate in `scan()` opens while the player still hasn't touched the keyboard, and the briefing then pages and eats the first character of their first *command* — issue #17 one screen later. I reproduced it (`srscan` → `rscan` → UNRECOGNIZED) before changing anything.

Three gates ran, and each found something the previous missed:

- **ui-review** approved the trade (banner top scrolls off) and caught that CI installs no tmux, so the new test would have reported SKIPPED on every PR while the job went green.
- **verifier** found the `asked = FALSE` mutant surviving — the test asserted that paging happens, not that it *keeps* happening, so a gate that switched off after page one would have passed.
- **code-review** found the placement blocker above, plus that the whole script passed with `TERM=dumb` forcing the classic fallback inside the pty — it wasn't testing curses at all — and that a private tmux socket isn't a private config, so `base-index 1` in a developer's `~/.tmux.conf` would fail the test and blame the game.

All four mutants now die, including the `scan()` placement.

**On #13 (TUI coverage in CI):** this PR already does the substance of it — `tests/tui.sh` drives real curses through a pty, ctest registers it, both runners install tmux, and the script hard-fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is set. What's left for #13 proper is breadth: the replay path, `freeze`/`thaw`, and the terminfo probe in `tui_terminal_capable()`, all of which the verifier exercised by hand but nothing covers automatically. I'll scope that once this lands.

the game had asked anything**, then ate the first letter of the answer:

Paging holds output back so it cannot scroll away unread. Before the
game has asked for a line there is nobody to hold it for, and the
keystroke such a pause waits for is the first one the player will type.
`skip()` now pages only once a prompt has been issued; the top of the
banner scrolls off instead, which is what any terminal too small to hold
it would do anyway.

**The flag is set in `readinput()`, not `scan()`** — and that is the
whole of it. Setup answers given on the command line (`sst -t tournament
5 long emeritus xyz`) are chewed out of a prefilled buffer that never
reaches `readinput()`, so a gate in `scan()` opens while the player is
still untouched by the keyboard; the briefing then pages and eats the
first character of their first *command*. Same bug, one screen later.
Hooking the line read is what makes "nobody is waiting yet" true on both
paths. My first cut got this backwards and code review caught it.

display, and nothing printed before the first prompt comes near its

journeys, command-line setup included.

curses, through tmux — at 80x24 and at the 72x24 minimum, plus the

**#17 is committed, pushed, and green** — 1Password came back on the retry.

[PR #24](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/pull/24), commit `d1c2cc5`, signature verified. All four CI legs pass, and I checked the logs rather than trusting the green: `Test #6: tui ... Passed` ran for real on **both** Ubuntu (6.9s) and macOS (9.6s) — it did not skip. That was the one thing neither the verifier nor code review could check locally, since neither had a macOS host, and it's exactly the failure mode the `$CI` hard-fail was built to prevent.

**What's next: #13, and it's now much smaller than it was filed.** This PR delivered its substance — tmux on both runners, curses driven through a real pty, and a test that can't silently skip. What's left is breadth, all of it exercised by hand during verification but not automated:

- the replay path (`quit` → `y` → second game, where the gate deliberately never resets)
- `freeze`/`thaw` via argv
- `tui_terminal_capable()`'s terminfo probe — the `TERM=dumb` and unknown-`TERM` fallbacks, which pipes can't reach

I'd fold that into #13 and close it out. After that, the open backlog is **#8** (indicate *why* the grid is masked), **#9** (terminal resize), **#14** (warnings, then `-Werror`), **#12** (seeded tournament journey), **#10** (osx.c header, good-first-issue), **#15** (dead `main.c` and Windows docs).

Two new issues also came out of the reviews and are worth filing before they're lost:

1. **The briefing and the end-of-game score never page at all.** Both build their text with `proutf()` containing embedded `\n`, which never increments `linecount`. At 80x24 a novice loses the top of the mission statement, and `quit` loses the score breakdown. Pre-existing on `main`, and it's the very next thing the player hits after the banner I just fixed.
2. **`prelim()` could fit 80x24 exactly.** Its content is only 10 lines; the overflow is entirely its leading `skip(2)` and three blank separators. Dropping those when the window is short would keep the whole ship visible instead of scrolling its nacelle off.

Want me to file those two and start #13?

input.command:
SP=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-super-star-trek/f543190f-4027-47a1-8fe2-512c2d383260/scratchpad
cat > $SP/issue-paging.md <<'EOF'
## Problem

Text printed with an embedded `\n` never counts towards paging, so two
of the longest passages in the game scroll away unread on a 24-line
terminal in `-t`: the mission briefing at the start of a game, and the
score breakdown at the end.

Reproduce (80x24, the size most emulators open at):

```sh
tmux -f /dev/null -L p new-session -d -x 80 -y 24 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep 60'
tmux -f /dev/null -L p send-keys -t t 'regular' Enter
tmux -f /dev/null -L p send-keys -t t 'short' Enter
tmux -f /dev/null -L p send-keys -t t 'novice' Enter
tmux -f /dev/null -L p send-keys -t t 'xyz' Enter
tmux -f /dev/null -L p capture-pane -t t -p
```

The novice briefing starts mid-sentence at `your mission.  As you
proceed you may be given more time.` — the stardate, the size of the
invasion force and the stardate allotment have all gone. `quit` is the
same: the score table scrolls past and only the `****` rule and `Do you
want to play again?` survive.

## Why it happens

`proutf()` (`sst.c:781`) formats into a buffer and hands the whole thing
to `proutn()`. Only `skip()` increments `linecount`, so a string
containing its own newlines advances the screen without advancing the
pager's idea of how full it is.

The two big offenders build their text that way:

- the briefing, `setup.c:380-397` (`It is stardate %d. The Federation is
  being attacked by\n` and the rest)
- the score, `finish.c:368-394` and the lines around them

## Why it matters

Both are text the player is meant to read. The briefing is the only
place the game states the mission and the deadline, and at novice skill
it is the tutorial. The score is the payoff for a whole game. In the
classic display the terminal's own scrollback makes this survivable; the
curses message window has no scrollback at all, so it is simply gone.

At 80x24 the briefing is the very next screen after the startup banner,
so a new player meets it immediately.

## Suggested approach

Worth weighing rather than picking blind:

- Make `proutf()` count the newlines it emits — pass the buffer through
  the same path `skip()` uses instead of straight to `proutn()`. Most
  faithful to the intent, but it changes paging behaviour everywhere
  `proutf` is used, so plain mode needs checking closely.
- Rewrite the two passages to use `prout()`/`skip()` per line. Local and
  obvious, but leaves the trap in place for the next caller.
- Have `tui_puts()` count newlines as they reach the window, which
  catches every route into the message area rather than just `proutf`.

Whichever is chosen, plain mode must not change as a side effect (see
AGENTS.md) — that is the constraint that makes this less trivial than it
looks, because the plain display pages at 23 lines and would start
pausing in places it never has.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At 80x24 in `-t`, the briefing can be read from its first line.
- [ ] At 80x24 in `-t`, the score table can be read from its first line.
- [ ] Paging elsewhere is unchanged.
- [ ] Plain mode output is byte-identical for a seeded (`tournament <n>`)
      journey, or the change and its reason are stated in the commit.
- [ ] `ctest --test-dir build` green, with coverage added to
      `tests/tui.sh` for whichever passage is fixed.

## Notes

Pre-existing since the TUI landed (#2); found by ui-review and the
verifier while fixing #17, which fixed the same class of problem for the
startup banner. Testing needs a pty — see AGENTS.md for the tmux recipe,
and note `tests/tui.sh` now drives it automatically.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).
EOF
gh issue create --title "TUI: the briefing and the score scroll away unread at 80x24" --label bug --body-file $SP/issue-paging.md 2>&1 | tail -2
input.description: File the proutf paging issue

input.command:
SP=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-super-star-trek/f543190f-4027-47a1-8fe2-512c2d383260/scratchpad
cat > $SP/issue-banner.md <<'EOF'
## Problem

At 80x24 the startup banner does not fit the ten-line message window, so
the top of the Enterprise scrolls off and the player's first sight of
full-screen mode is a fragment:

```
               ||     / /    `--'
             __||____/ /_
            |___         \
                `--------'
   THE USS ENTERPRISE --- NCC-1701
```

The nacelle and hull are gone. What is left reads as a rendering fault
rather than as deliberate art.

## Why it happens

`prelim()` (`setup.c:5-20`) emits 15 counted lines, but only **10 of
them carry content**: seven lines of art, `THE USS ENTERPRISE ---
NCC-1701`, `-SUPER- STAR TREK`, and `Latest update-21 Sept 78`. The
overflow is entirely whitespace — the leading `skip(2)` and the three
blank separators between the three closing lines.

`tui_pageheight()` is exactly 10 at 24 rows. So the banner fits the
window precisely, if the blank lines go.

## Why it matters

80x24 is the classic default and the common first run of `sst -t`. This
is the first thing the game draws, and the ship is the single piece of
art in it.

## Suggested approach

Drop the separators when the message window is too short to afford them
— roughly, when `tui_pageheight() < 15` — and keep the current spacing
everywhere else. Plain mode has 23 lines and must keep its current
output exactly.

Note that `prelim()` is in `setup.c` and has no business knowing about
curses; the height query belongs behind the existing `tui_pageheight()`
call, which already returns a sensible value in both modes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At 80x24 in `-t`, the whole banner is visible when the game asks
      its first question.
- [ ] At 72x24 (the minimum) the same holds, or the art degrades
      deliberately rather than by accident.
- [ ] At a comfortable size (100x30) the banner is unchanged.
- [ ] Plain mode output is byte-identical for a seeded (`tournament <n>`)
      journey.
- [ ] `ctest --test-dir build` green; add the check to `tests/tui.sh`.

## Notes

Raised by ui-review while fixing #17. That fix stopped the pager pausing
mid-banner, which is why the top now scrolls instead — the right trade,
but this makes the trade unnecessary. Cosmetic, and a good candidate for
someone wanting a small self-contained change.

Testing needs a pty — see AGENTS.md for the tmux recipe; `tests/tui.sh`
does it automatically.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).
EOF
gh issue create --title "TUI: make the startup banner fit an 80x24 window" --label "enhancement,good first issue" --body-file $SP/issue-banner.md 2>&1 | tail -2

title:	Add TUI coverage to CI
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	enhancement
comments:	1
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:

number:	13
--
## Goal

Give CI some coverage of the full-screen interface. Today it has none: the workflow builds `tui.c`/`tuifmt.c` and runs the formatter unit tests, but nothing ever launches `sst -t`, so the curses layer itself is only ever exercised by hand.

## Blocked by

#5 — while piping into `sst -t` hangs, every non-interactive invocation is a CI hang rather than a test.

## Suggested approach

Two levels, either or both:

1. **Cheap, no pty.** Once the non-tty fallback lands, assert that `sst -t` with piped input falls back to plain mode, plays, and exits 0. This needs no extra tooling and would have caught the hang.
2. **Real pty via tmux.** Drive an actual full-screen session and assert on captured panes — the quadrant/status panels render, a command updates them, the terminal is restored on exit. AGENTS.md documents the recipe (`tmux new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 …`, `send-keys`, `capture-pane`).

Level 2 is the more valuable coverage and the more flake-prone: it depends on sleeps and timing. If you take it, make the waits condition-based (poll `capture-pane` until the expected text appears, with a bounded overall timeout) rather than fixed `sleep`s, and keep it out of the critical path if it proves unstable. `tmux` is available on GitHub's Ubuntu and macOS runners but should not be assumed — install or skip explicitly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CI exercises `-t` in some form on at least Linux.
- [ ] No fixed-`sleep`-based races: 20 consecutive runs pass.
- [ ] Failures produce useful diagnostics (captured pane content), not just a timeout.
- [ ] Bounded by a CTest `TIMEOUT` so a hang fails fast instead of burning the job budget.

## Notes

Never redirect the game's stdout inside a tmux session — it breaks curses rendering. See AGENTS.md.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

#!/bin/sh
# Drives the full-screen display through a real terminal.
#
# Everything else in the suite talks to the game through pipes, which
# is enough for the fallback path but never exercises curses itself.
# This one runs the game inside tmux so there is a genuine pty, and
# reads the screen back the way a player would see it.
#
# The size matters. 80x24 is what most terminal emulators open at and
# 72x24 is the smallest the TUI accepts; at both the message window is
# only ten lines, so the startup banner overflows it -- which is how
# the pager came to be waiting for a keystroke before the game had
# asked the player anything, and to eat the first letter of the answer.
#
# Usage: tui.sh /path/to/sst
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) when there is no tmux to run in.
#
# Needs a sleep that takes a fraction, which GNU and BSD both have but
# POSIX does not promise; busybox would need whole seconds.

set -u

SST="${1:-./sst}"
case "$SST" in
	/*) ;;
	*) SST="$(pwd)/$SST" ;;
esac
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)

if ! command -v tmux >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	# A developer without tmux gets a skip. CI does not: this is the
	# only test that runs curses at all, and a green build that quietly
	# skipped it would be worse than no test.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ]; then
		echo "FAIL: tmux is missing on CI, so the TUI went untested" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: tmux is not installed, so there is no pty to test in" >&2
	exit 77
fi
if [ ! -x "$SST" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $SST is not executable" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Run on a socket of our own, never the default one. A developer's tmux
# server is usually sitting on the default socket with a day's real work
# in it, and anything server-wide -- this script's cleanup, or an agent
# tidying up after driving the TUI by hand -- takes that down too. -L
# buys a private server, so cleanup can be as blunt as it needs to be.
socket="sst-tui-$$"
session="tui"
pane="$session:0.0"

# -f /dev/null as well as -L: a private socket is not a private config,
# and `set -g base-index 1` -- one of the commoner things people put in
# ~/.tmux.conf -- moves the pane out from under the name used below, so
# every capture comes back empty and the game gets blamed for it.
tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }

# tmux leaves the socket file behind when the server exits, so a suite
# that ran often would slowly fill the directory with dead ones. This is
# where tmux puts them on both Linux and macOS: $TMUX_TMPDIR if it is
# set, /tmp otherwise.
cleanup() {
	tm kill-server 2>/dev/null
	rm -f "${TMUX_TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-$(id -u)/$socket"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'cleanup; exit 130' INT
trap 'cleanup; exit 143' TERM
trap 'cleanup; exit 129' HUP

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

screen() { tm capture-pane -t "$pane" -p 2>/dev/null; }

dump() {
	printf '  --- screen ---\n' >&2
	screen | sed 's/^/  | /' >&2
}

# Wait until the screen shows $1, up to about eight seconds. Polling
# beats a fixed sleep: curses paints in its own time, and a machine
# under load should not turn into a failure.
wait_for() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 80 ]; do
		if screen | grep -qF "$1"; then return 0; fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.1
	done
	return 1
}

# Answer any paging prompts until the command prompt comes back. A
# space is only ever sent while a pause is actually showing, so this
# cannot quietly paper over a pause that should not have been there.
to_command() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
		screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND' && return 0
		if screen | grep -qE 'CONTINUE|HIT SPACE BAR'; then
			tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
		fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.25
	done
	return 1
}

want() {
	screen | grep -qF "$2" || { fail "$1"; dump; }
}

unwanted() {
	if screen | grep -qF "$2"; then fail "$1"; dump; fi
}

# tmux takes a shell command line, not an argument list, so the path
# has to survive being quoted into one.
sstq=$(printf "%s" "$SST" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g")

# Start the game on a terminal $1 wide by $2 tall, passing $3 (if any)
# on the command line. It reads sst.doc from the current directory, and
# dies with the session.
start() {
	cleanup
	tm new-session -d -x "$1" -y "$2" -s "$session" -c "$srcdir" \
		"'$sstq' -t ${3:-}; sleep 30" 2>/dev/null || {
		echo "FAIL: could not start a ${1}x${2} tmux session" >&2
		exit 1
	}
}

# --- the game asks before it pauses, at every size it accepts -------
# 80x24 is what most emulators open at; 72x24 is the smallest the TUI
# will run in. The banner is longer than the message window at both, so
# it scrolls -- ordinary. Stopping to ask for a keystroke is not:
# nothing has been asked yet, so there is no reader to wait for, and
# the prompt sits exactly where the player is about to type an answer.
for size in 80x24 72x24; do
	cols=${size%x*}
	rows=${size#*x}
	start "$cols" "$rows"

	if ! wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'; then
		fail "$size: the game never asked its first question"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	# Curses is really running, not the classic display falling back
	# inside the pty. Without this every assertion below is satisfied
	# by the plain path, and a broken tui_init() would still look
	# green -- from a script whose whole point is to exercise curses.
	# The panel titles are drawn in TUI mode and nowhere else.
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Status "
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Quadrant "

	unwanted "$size: paused with [HIT SPACE BAR] before asking anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	unwanted "$size: paused with [CONTINUE?] before asking anything" "[CONTINUE?]"

	# With a pager waiting, its getch() swallowed the leading
	# character and the game saw "egular".
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'regular' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Short, Medium, or Long'; then
		fail "$size: the game did not accept 'regular' as the first answer"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	unwanted "$size: the first answer lost a character" 'What is "'
done

# --- paging still works once the game is running --------------------
# Carrying on from the 72x24 game above: the rest of setup, then the
# briefing, which does page.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'short' Enter
wait_for 'Novice, Fair, Good, Expert' || fail "setup did not reach the skill question"
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'novice' Enter
sleep 0.5
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'xyz' Enter
if ! to_command; then
	fail "the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
	exit 1
fi

# A manual entry runs well past the ten-line message window, so it has
# to page -- the fix must only have quietened the pauses nobody asked
# for, not the ones that do the job.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'help move' Enter
if ! wait_for 'CONTINUE'; then
	fail "long output no longer pages"
	dump
fi
# And the pause really does hold: still there a moment later, waiting,
# rather than having flashed past on its own.
sleep 0.5
want "the paging prompt did not wait for a keystroke" "CONTINUE"

# One keystroke buys one screen, not the whole entry. A gate that
# switched paging off again after the first pause would let the rest of
# the manual scroll away, and answering pauses until the prompt returns
# would not notice: the manual runs to several screens, so the command
# prompt must not be back yet.
# Watched for a few seconds rather than sampled once: a single look
# after a fixed sleep passes on a machine that has not repainted yet.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 16 ]; do
	if screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND'; then
		fail "the manual stopped paging after its first screen"
		dump
		break
	fi
	i=$((i + 1))
	sleep 0.25
done

# Spaces get it moving again -- however many pages the entry runs to.
to_command || fail "the manual never finished paging"

# The game is still listening. Long-range scan says something the
# always-on panels never do, so this cannot pass on their text.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
	fail "the game did not carry on after the paging prompt"
	dump
fi

# --- setup answered on the command line ------------------------------
# The same bug reaches further than the banner. With the setup answers
# in argv the player never types during setup at all, so the game runs
# on into the briefing -- and a pause there waits for, and eats, the
# first character of their first command.
#
# The briefing's fixed text is already longer than the window, so the
# case does not rest on the galaxy that gets generated; the seed only
# decides how much further past the threshold it goes, and rand()
# differing between C libraries can blunt that but not invert it. A
# pause before the player has touched the keyboard is wrong either way.
start 80 24 'tournament 5 long emeritus xyz'
if ! wait_for 'COMMAND'; then
	fail "argv setup: the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
else
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "CONTINUE"

#!/bin/sh
# Drives the full-screen display through a real terminal.
#
# Everything else in the suite talks to the game through pipes, which
# is enough for the fallback path but never exercises curses itself.
# This one runs the game inside tmux so there is a genuine pty, and
# reads the screen back the way a player would see it.
#
# The size matters. 80x24 is what most terminal emulators open at and
# 72x24 is the smallest the TUI accepts; at both the message window is
# only ten lines, so the startup banner overflows it -- which is how
# the pager came to be waiting for a keystroke before the game had
# asked the player anything, and to eat the first letter of the answer.
#
# Usage: tui.sh /path/to/sst
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) when there is no tmux to run in.
#
# Needs a sleep that takes a fraction, which GNU and BSD both have but
# POSIX does not promise; busybox would need whole seconds.

set -u

SST="${1:-./sst}"
case "$SST" in
	/*) ;;
	*) SST="$(pwd)/$SST" ;;
esac
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)

if ! command -v tmux >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	# A developer without tmux gets a skip. CI does not: this is the
	# only test that runs curses at all, and a green build that quietly
	# skipped it would be worse than no test.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ]; then
		echo "FAIL: tmux is missing on CI, so the TUI went untested" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: tmux is not installed, so there is no pty to test in" >&2
	exit 77
fi
if [ ! -x "$SST" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $SST is not executable" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Run on a socket of our own, never the default one. A developer's tmux
# server is usually sitting on the default socket with a day's real work
# in it, and anything server-wide -- this script's cleanup, or an agent
# tidying up after driving the TUI by hand -- takes that down too. -L
# buys a private server, so cleanup can be as blunt as it needs to be.
socket="sst-tui-$$"
session="tui"
pane="$session:0.0"

# -f /dev/null as well as -L: a private socket is not a private config,
# and `set -g base-index 1` -- one of the commoner things people put in
# ~/.tmux.conf -- moves the pane out from under the name used below, so
# every capture comes back empty and the game gets blamed for it.
tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }

# tmux leaves the socket file behind when the server exits, so a suite
# that ran often would slowly fill the directory with dead ones. This is
# where tmux puts them on both Linux and macOS: $TMUX_TMPDIR if it is
# set, /tmp otherwise.
cleanup() {
	tm kill-server 2>/dev/null
	rm -f "${TMUX_TMPDIR:-/tmp}/tmux-$(id -u)/$socket"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'cleanup; exit 130' INT
trap 'cleanup; exit 143' TERM
trap 'cleanup; exit 129' HUP

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

screen() { tm capture-pane -t "$pane" -p 2>/dev/null; }

dump() {
	printf '  --- screen ---\n' >&2
	screen | sed 's/^/  | /' >&2
}

# Wait until the screen shows $1, up to about eight seconds. Polling
# beats a fixed sleep: curses paints in its own time, and a machine
# under load should not turn into a failure.
wait_for() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 80 ]; do
		if screen | grep -qF "$1"; then return 0; fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.1
	done
	return 1
}

# Answer any paging prompts until the command prompt comes back. A
# space is only ever sent while a pause is actually showing, so this
# cannot quietly paper over a pause that should not have been there.
to_command() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
		screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND' && return 0
		if screen | grep -qE 'CONTINUE|HIT SPACE BAR'; then
			tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
		fi
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.25
	done
	return 1
}

want() {
	screen | grep -qF "$2" || { fail "$1"; dump; }
}

unwanted() {
	if screen | grep -qF "$2"; then fail "$1"; dump; fi
}

# tmux takes a shell command line, not an argument list, so the path
# has to survive being quoted into one.
sstq=$(printf "%s" "$SST" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g")

# Start the game on a terminal $1 wide by $2 tall, passing $3 (if any)
# on the command line and running it under $4 (if any, an `env ...`
# prefix). It reads sst.doc from the current directory, and dies with
# the session.
start() {
	cleanup
	tm new-session -d -x "$1" -y "$2" -s "$session" -c "$srcdir" \
		"${4:-} '$sstq' -t ${3:-}; sleep 30" 2>/dev/null || {
		echo "FAIL: could not start a ${1}x${2} tmux session" >&2
		exit 1
	}
}

# --- the game asks before it pauses, at every size it accepts -------
# 80x24 is what most emulators open at; 72x24 is the smallest the TUI
# will run in. The banner is longer than the message window at both, so
# it scrolls -- ordinary. Stopping to ask for a keystroke is not:
# nothing has been asked yet, so there is no reader to wait for, and
# the prompt sits exactly where the player is about to type an answer.
for size in 80x24 72x24; do
	cols=${size%x*}
	rows=${size#*x}
	start "$cols" "$rows"

	if ! wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'; then
		fail "$size: the game never asked its first question"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	# Curses is really running, not the classic display falling back
	# inside the pty. Without this every assertion below is satisfied
	# by the plain path, and a broken tui_init() would still look
	# green -- from a script whose whole point is to exercise curses.
	# The panel titles are drawn in TUI mode and nowhere else.
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Status "
	want "$size: the full-screen display never came up" " Quadrant "

	unwanted "$size: paused with [HIT SPACE BAR] before asking anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	unwanted "$size: paused with [CONTINUE?] before asking anything" "[CONTINUE?]"

	# With a pager waiting, its getch() swallowed the leading
	# character and the game saw "egular".
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'regular' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Short, Medium, or Long'; then
		fail "$size: the game did not accept 'regular' as the first answer"
		dump
		exit 1
	fi
	unwanted "$size: the first answer lost a character" 'What is "'
done

# --- paging still works once the game is running --------------------
# Carrying on from the 72x24 game above: the rest of setup, then the
# briefing, which does page.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'short' Enter
wait_for 'Novice, Fair, Good, Expert' || fail "setup did not reach the skill question"
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'novice' Enter
sleep 0.5
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'xyz' Enter
if ! to_command; then
	fail "the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
	exit 1
fi

# A manual entry runs well past the ten-line message window, so it has
# to page -- the fix must only have quietened the pauses nobody asked
# for, not the ones that do the job.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'help move' Enter
if ! wait_for 'CONTINUE'; then
	fail "long output no longer pages"
	dump
fi
# And the pause really does hold: still there a moment later, waiting,
# rather than having flashed past on its own.
sleep 0.5
want "the paging prompt did not wait for a keystroke" "CONTINUE"

# One keystroke buys one screen, not the whole entry. A gate that
# switched paging off again after the first pause would let the rest of
# the manual scroll away, and answering pauses until the prompt returns
# would not notice: the manual runs to several screens, so the command
# prompt must not be back yet.
# Watched for a few seconds rather than sampled once: a single look
# after a fixed sleep passes on a machine that has not repainted yet.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" Space
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 16 ]; do
	if screen | grep -qF 'COMMAND'; then
		fail "the manual stopped paging after its first screen"
		dump
		break
	fi
	i=$((i + 1))
	sleep 0.25
done

# Spaces get it moving again -- however many pages the entry runs to.
to_command || fail "the manual never finished paging"

# The game is still listening. Long-range scan says something the
# always-on panels never do, so this cannot pass on their text.
tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
	fail "the game did not carry on after the paging prompt"
	dump
fi

# --- setup answered on the command line ------------------------------
# The same bug reaches further than the banner. With the setup answers
# in argv the player never types during setup at all, so the game runs
# on into the briefing -- and a pause there waits for, and eats, the
# first character of their first command.
#
# The briefing's fixed text is already longer than the window, so the
# case does not rest on the galaxy that gets generated; the seed only
# decides how much further past the threshold it goes, and rand()
# differing between C libraries can blunt that but not invert it. A
# pause before the player has touched the keyboard is wrong either way.
start 80 24 'tournament 5 long emeritus xyz'
if ! wait_for 'COMMAND'; then
	fail "argv setup: the game never reached its command prompt"
	dump
else
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "CONTINUE"
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	# Long-range scan rather than short: its heading appears only in
	# the message window, so waiting for it proves the command was
	# read whole. Sampling the screen after a fixed sleep instead
	# would pass on a slow machine that had not repainted yet.
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
		fail "argv setup: the first command was not accepted"
		dump
	fi
	unwanted "argv setup: the first command lost a character" "UNRECOGNIZED"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'tui OK\n'

# Drives the full-screen display through a real terminal.
#
# Everything else in the suite talks to the game through pipes, which
# is enough for the fallback path but never exercises curses itself.
# This one runs the game inside tmux so there is a genuine pty, and
# reads the screen back the way a player would see it.
#
# The size matters. 80x24 is what most terminal emulators open at and
# 72x24 is the smallest the TUI accepts; at both the message window is
# only ten lines, so the startup banner overflows it -- which is how
# the pager came to be waiting for a keystroke before the game had
# asked the player anything, and to eat the first letter of the answer.
#
# Usage: tui.sh /path/to/sst
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) when there is no tmux to run in.
#
# Needs a sleep that takes a fraction, which GNU and BSD both have but
# POSIX does not promise; busybox would need whole seconds.

set -u

input.prompt:
Review the change on branch `test/tui-ci-coverage` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek. It is one uncommitted file: `tests/tui.sh` (see `git diff`).

Context: this closes issue #13, "Add TUI coverage to CI". The branch is stacked on `fix/tui-first-keystroke` (PR #24, green, not yet merged), which introduced `tests/tui.sh` and installed tmux on both CI runners. This change is **test-only** — no game code is touched.

What it adds to the existing script (which already covered first-run at 80x24 and 72x24, paging, and setup answered on the command line):
- **replay**: quit → score questions → play again → a second game, asserting the panels show the new game rather than a frame left over from the last one (the class of bug #21 fixed).
- **freeze/thaw**: play, `freeze sav`, then start again with `frozen sav`, asserting the panels show the thawed game and its first command is accepted whole. Played in a temp dir so no `.trk` lands in the source tree.
- **two refusals only a real terminal can produce**: `TERM=dumb` (curses starts but cannot address the cursor — what Emacs' shell buffer sets) and a 70x20 terminal (below the 72x24 minimum). Both must print their notice, must NOT draw panels, and must carry on playing in the classic display.

You are an expert in games and CLI games. Since this is a test, what I most want from you is a **player's-eye judgement of whether the assertions describe behaviour a player would actually care about, and whether anything a player would notice is still uncovered**. Specifically:
- Are the fallback notices well-worded and does the fallback experience actually work end-to-end (not just print a line)? Play them.
- Is the replay experience right — does the second game feel clean, panels and all?
- Does thawing a saved game present correctly in full-screen mode?
- Is there a player-visible TUI behaviour still untested that should be in this slice, versus one that deserves its own issue?

Testing needs a pty. Use tmux **on your own socket via `-L <unique-name>` and with `-f /dev/null`** — never the default socket, never a bare `kill-server`, never `kill-session` on a session you did not create. Never redirect the game's stdout in a tmux session. The build is at ./build. Remove any `*.trk` files you leave in the repo root.

Report findings only; do not edit files.

content.text:
## Verdict

**Acceptable with should-fix items.** The three journeys this adds are the right ones — replay, freeze/thaw, and the two refusals only a pty can produce are all things a player hits and all things that broke before (#18, #21). I drove every one of them by hand and the *behaviour* is genuinely good: both fallbacks print a sane notice and then play a complete, fully usable classic game (including paging, which I answered with the space bar); the second game's panels blank between games and refill with the new quadrant; a thawed game presents correctly at both 80x24 and 72x24 and takes its first command whole. The problem is with two of the *assertions*: the quadrant-panel check cannot fail for the bug it names, and the most player-visible half of #21 — panels still showing the finished game while the next one is being set up — is never checked. There is also one uncovered behaviour I'd argue belongs in this slice ahead of freeze/thaw: nothing verifies the panels ever *update*.

## Findings

**1. should-fix — the quadrant-panel assertion is vacuous (replay and thaw).**
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh:321` and `:352`

```sh
want "replay: the quadrant panel is not showing a quadrant" "Quadrant "
want "thaw: the quadrant panel is empty" "Quadrant "
```

`tui_refresh_panels()` in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c` writes the box title `" Quadrant "` *before* it knows whether a game is running, and only overwrites it with `" Quadrant %d - %d "` when `tui_ingame`. So `grep -F "Quadrant "` matches the exact empty-frame state the check exists to catch. I confirmed this on a real capture of the blank-panel state: `grep -c "Quadrant "` → 1, `grep -c "Stardate"` → 0. The `Stardate` half of each pair is sound; the quadrant half is not. Suggest a regex form, e.g. a `want_re` helper asserting `' Quadrant [0-9]+ - [0-9]+ '`. Stronger still: the briefing prints `The Enterprise is currently in Quadrant X - Y`, so you can scrape that off the message window and assert the panel title says the same thing — that catches a *stale* panel as well as a blank one, which the current check cannot.

**2. should-fix — the visible half of #21 is unasserted.**
`tests/tui.sh:298-306`. After `y` at "play again", the game re-asks "regular, tournament, or frozen?" while the panels are (correctly) blank — I verified this. That moment, a player answering setup questions with the *previous* captain's quadrant still framed above them, is the failure #21 was reported as. The block only does `unwanted ... "CONTINUE"` there. Add, right after the `wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'`:

```sh
unwanted "replay: the finished game is still on the panels" "Stardate"
```

**3. should-fix (coverage gap, arguably in this slice) — nothing asserts the panels ever update.**
The always-on scan and status readout are the entire point of `-t`, and `tests/test_tuifmt.c` only covers the formatters, not that `tui_refresh_panels()` is still called after a command. I confirmed by hand at 72x24 that `move 1 0` updates the title (`Quadrant 4 - 6` → `4 - 7`), `Position`, `Energy`, `Time Left` and the `E` marker — but if that call were dropped tomorrow every assertion in this script would still pass. It is a few lines: capture `Position`, send `move 1 0`, poll until `Position` differs. I'd rank this above the freeze/thaw case in value.

**4. nit — the post-`freeze` `to_command` cannot fail.**
`tests/tui.sh:339`. `COMMAND>` is still on screen from the prompt the player typed at, so `to_command` returns on the stale text; the check "the game did not come back after freezing" is decorative. The real assertion is the `sav.trk` existence test below it, which is fine. Either drop the check or wait for a second prompt.

**5. nit — the replay block runs unconditionally on a session it did not start.**
If the argv-setup block fails, `tm send-keys 'quit'` at `tests/tui.sh:290` goes into whatever prompt is up and produces a cascade of confusing failures for whoever reads the CI log. Guard it on the argv block's success, or start a fresh session for the replay.

**6. nit — the replay journey plays in the source tree, one keystroke from littering it.**
`Do you want your score recorded?` answered `y` calls `freeze(FALSE)`, which writes a `.trk` next to the cwd — and that block still runs with `startdir="$srcdir"`. The script answers `n`, so nothing lands today (verified: repo clean after a full run), but since `$work` already exists, running the whole script from `$work` with `sst.doc` copied or symlinked in would remove the hazard entirely.

**7. nit — wording inconsistency the test now pins in a second place.**
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:461` says "using **the** classic display"; `:464` says "using classic display". `tests/journey.sh:159` already carries a comment apologising for it, and `tui.sh` now matches on `"Terminal too small"` alone. The "short" justification does not really hold — the full wording is 61 columns and the notice already prints on a 70-column terminal. Suggest normalising `sst.c:464` and relaxing `journey.sh` to match the common phrasing.

## Uncovered, and where I'd put it

- **Own issue — no SIGWINCH handling.** Growing a 72x24 game to 100x30 leaves the panels stuck at their original width with dead space to the right; shrinking to 60x20 truncates the panel borders mid-line and leaves two stacked `COMMAND>` prompts. Pre-existing, not caused by this branch, but very visible and worth filing.
- **Own issue — the too-small fallback pages at 23 lines.** On the 70x20 terminal the test uses, `help move` loses the first three lines of every page before `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` appears (I watched `Spock- "Captain, I've found..."` and the `Mnemonic:` header scroll away unread). Plain mode has always assumed 23 lines, but the new "Terminal too small" branch is the path that deliberately routes short terminals there.
- **Nit / follow-up — thawing a missing file in `-t`.** `sst -t frozen nosuch` prints `Can't find game file nosuch.trk` and drops cleanly back to the first setup question with blank panels. It works, it is the likeliest typo in the new freeze/thaw journey, and it is two lines to assert.
- **Own issue — colour (#23) is unverified.** `capture-pane -e` would let this script assert the quadrant grid and status panel are actually coloured.
- **Minor — the new cases only run at 80x24.** AGENTS.md asks for 72x24 as well. I checked the thawed game at 72x24 by hand and it renders correctly, so the risk is low, but wrapping the thaw case in the existing size loop is cheap.

## Verdict

**Acceptable with should-fix items.** The three journeys this adds are the right ones — replay, freeze/thaw, and the two refusals only a pty can produce are all things a player hits and all things that broke before (#18, #21). I drove every one of them by hand and the *behaviour* is genuinely good: both fallbacks print a sane notice and then play a complete, fully usable classic game (including paging, which I answered with the space bar); the second game's panels blank between games and refill with the new quadrant; a thawed game presents correctly at both 80x24 and 72x24 and takes its first command whole. The problem is with two of the *assertions*: the quadrant-panel check cannot fail for the bug it names, and the most player-visible half of #21 — panels still showing the finished game while the next one is being set up — is never checked. There is also one uncovered behaviour I'd argue belongs in this slice ahead of freeze/thaw: nothing verifies the panels ever *update*.

## Findings

**1. should-fix — the quadrant-panel assertion is vacuous (replay and thaw).**
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh:321` and `:352`

```sh
want "replay: the quadrant panel is not showing a quadrant" "Quadrant "
want "thaw: the quadrant panel is empty" "Quadrant "
```

`tui_refresh_panels()` in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c` writes the box title `" Quadrant "` *before* it knows whether a game is running, and only overwrites it with `" Quadrant %d - %d "` when `tui_ingame`. So `grep -F "Quadrant "` matches the exact empty-frame state the check exists to catch. I confirmed this on a real capture of the blank-panel state: `grep -c "Quadrant "` → 1, `grep -c "Stardate"` → 0. The `Stardate` half of each pair is sound; the quadrant half is not. Suggest a regex form, e.g. a `want_re` helper asserting `' Quadrant [0-9]+ - [0-9]+ '`. Stronger still: the briefing prints `The Enterprise is currently in Quadrant X - Y`, so you can scrape that off the message window and assert the panel title says the same thing — that catches a *stale* panel as well as a blank one, which the current check cannot.

**2. should-fix — the visible half of #21 is unasserted.**
`tests/tui.sh:298-306`. After `y` at "play again", the game re-asks "regular, tournament, or frozen?" while the panels are (correctly) blank — I verified this. That moment, a player answering setup questions with the *previous* captain's quadrant still framed above them, is the failure #21 was reported as. The block only does `unwanted ... "CONTINUE"` there. Add, right after the `wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'`:

```sh
unwanted "replay: the finished game is still on the panels" "Stardate"
```

**3. should-fix (coverage gap, arguably in this slice) — nothing asserts the panels ever update.**
The always-on scan and status readout are the entire point of `-t`, and `tests/test_tuifmt.c` only covers the formatters, not that `tui_refresh_panels()` is still called after a command. I confirmed by hand at 72x24 that `move 1 0` updates the title (`Quadrant 4 - 6` → `4 - 7`), `Position`, `Energy`, `Time Left` and the `E` marker — but if that call were dropped tomorrow every assertion in this script would still pass. It is a few lines: capture `Position`, send `move 1 0`, poll until `Position` differs. I'd rank this above the freeze/thaw case in value.

**4. nit — the post-`freeze` `to_command` cannot fail.**
`tests/tui.sh:339`. `COMMAND>` is still on screen from the prompt the player typed at, so `to_command` returns on the stale text; the check "the game did not come back after freezing" is decorative. The real assertion is the `sav.trk` existence test below it, which is fine. Either drop the check or wait for a second prompt.

**5. nit — the replay block runs unconditionally on a session it did not start.**
If the argv-setup block fails, `tm send-keys 'quit'` at `tests/tui.sh:290` goes into whatever prompt is up and produces a cascade of confusing failures for whoever reads the CI log. Guard it on the argv block's success, or start a fresh session for the replay.

**6. nit — the replay journey plays in the source tree, one keystroke from littering it.**
`Do you want your score recorded?` answered `y` calls `freeze(FALSE)`, which writes a `.trk` next to the cwd — and that block still runs with `startdir="$srcdir"`. The script answers `n`, so nothing lands today (verified: repo clean after a full run), but since `$work` already exists, running the whole script from `$work` with `sst.doc` copied or symlinked in would remove the hazard entirely.

**7. nit — wording inconsistency the test now pins in a second place.**
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:461` says "using **the** classic display"; `:464` says "using classic display". `tests/journey.sh:159` already carries a comment apologising for it, and `tui.sh` now matches on `"Terminal too small"` alone. The "short" justification does not really hold — the full wording is 61 columns and the notice already prints on a 70-column terminal. Suggest normalising `sst.c:464` and relaxing `journey.sh` to match the common phrasing.

else
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "CONTINUE"
	unwanted "argv setup: paused before the player had typed anything" "HIT SPACE BAR"
	# Long-range scan rather than short: its heading appears only in
	# the message window, so waiting for it proves the command was
	# read whole. Sampling the screen after a fixed sleep instead
	# would pass on a slow machine that had not repainted yet.
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'Long-range scan for Quadrant'; then
		fail "argv setup: the first command was not accepted"
		dump
	fi
	unwanted "argv setup: the first command lost a character" "UNRECOGNIZED"
fi
