input.content:
test: record what the game does, so a change to it is visible

The suite asked whether things happened -- a game docked, nothing
desynchronised, no developer chatter got out -- and never whether a
number was right. Nothing checked combat arithmetic, time accounting,
what a starbase gives back, or the score. A change to any of it was
invisible unless it crashed or stopped a journey.

That is how the Super-commander came to spend decades pursuing along
the wrong axis with eight tests, twelve seeded games and a mutation
battery watching: none of them knows what correct movement looks like.
It took someone reading the line.

So: seven journeys played to a fixed script and recorded byte for byte.
Any difference is a failure. They cannot say the game is right; they
say exactly what changed, which is the question a reviewer actually
has. Between them they read every report, compute an arrival time,
cross quadrants, take and give fire, destroy Klingons with aimed
torpedoes, spend a ship dry and have a starbase fill it up again,
freeze and thaw, and end a game with the score sheet.

None of that was possible a commit ago. Recordings of a seeded game
meant nothing across platforms while the generator was the C library's;
now that it is the game's own, a fixture holds on both CI legs.

Proof that it bites: applying the one-character fix for #42 changes the
combat recording and nothing else. Whoever takes that issue now gets to
show which games moved rather than argue the Super-commander looks
better.

Proof that it does not bite on everything, which matters just as much:
adding a unit to the torpedo damage kills the same Klingon and prints
the same line, and no recording notices. These are characterizations,
not proofs, and the file says so.

Recording is fussy on purpose. A journey is only recorded if the game
exited zero, produced a plausible amount of output, reached the
farewell, did not run out of input, printed no debug chatter and left
no carriage return at the end of a line -- otherwise --update refuses
and exits non-zero, rather than enshrining a crash as the new truth.
AGENTS.md says what a red golden test means and that re-recording is
not how to answer it.

**#42 is now a one-command demonstration.** Applying its one-character fix changes the `combat` recording and nothing else. Whoever takes it stops arguing that the Super-commander looks better and shows which games moved.

Hence the aimed journey.

- `--update` would have recorded a **segfaulting stub** as the new truth and exited 0. It now refuses unless the game exited clean, reached the farewell, kept its input, printed no debug chatter and left no stray carriage return.
- My `ending` journey **never ended the game** — a stray `y` got the self-destruct password rejected, so the death narration and score sheet weren't recorded at all, in the journey whose whole purpose was to record them.
- `computer 1` was a parse error, so the ETA arithmetic went unrecorded in the journey claiming to cover "the whole read-only surface".

`AGENTS.md` now carries the rule that matters most here: a red `golden` is explained in the commit, never re-recorded to turn CI green.

## Where the game stands

The suite went from *"did it crash"* to *"what changed"*. Known gap, written into the file: no journey manages to get the ship damaged, so device damage and repair are still unrecorded — I scanned 70 seeds looking for one and didn't find it.

The natural next move is **#42**, as the first fix to prove itself against the new machinery. After that, #46 (resize repaint) and #38 (`osx.c` declarations) are what remain.

## Goal

Unit-test the game's rules: the arithmetic and the decisions, asked
directly, with stated inputs and an expected answer.

## Why the current suite is not that

The suite is now good at two things and does neither of them.

`tests/golden.sh` records what the game does and reports what changed.
That catches a regression but cannot say a number is *wrong* — it only
knows what it used to be. Recording a bug is exactly as easy as
recording correct behaviour, and #42 was recorded for decades.

Everything else (`journey.sh`, `tournament.sh`, `tui.sh`, `eof.sh`,
`help.sh`) asks whether things *happened*: that a game docked, that
nothing desynchronised, that no developer chatter got out. Useful, and
not the same question.

The only place the suite states what an answer *should* be is
`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, and everything it checks is display.

So: nothing in the repository says what the game's rules are. Whether
combat damage, damage repair, time accounting, enemy movement or the
score come out right is currently a matter of reading the code.

## Why it is not simply a matter of writing them

The rules are not reachable on their own. Two obstacles, both of which
the codebase already shows the way around:

1. **Global state.** The game runs on ~90 globals declared through the
   `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`, so any test has to compose a
   whole game before asking a question. `tests/test_tuifmt.c` does this
   already: it defines `INCLUDED`, includes `sst.h`, and has a
   `basestate()` that sets up a plausible ship and quadrant. That
   pattern extends.

2. **Arithmetic tangled with output.** The rules are written amid the
   prose that describes them -- `battle.c` alone has 194 calls to
   `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`scan`, `moving.c` 135, `finish.c` 151. A
   function that both computes and narrates cannot be asked a question
   without capturing its narration.

   The way out is the one `tuifmt.c` already took: pull the decision
   into a function that computes and says nothing, and leave the
   narration where it was. `condition_now()` and `sensors_masked()`
   are both this -- extracted so a test could ask them, with the
   comment explaining why.

## Suggested approach

Incremental, one rule at a time, each with the golden recordings as
the safety net: extract a pure function, confirm the recordings do not
move, then write the test. If a recording *does* move, the extraction
changed behaviour and is wrong.

Worth doing in roughly this order, easiest and most valuable first:

- **Galaxy invariants** (`setup.c`). After setup, the Klingons,
  starbases and stars encoded in `d.galaxy` should sum to `inkling`,
  `inbase`, `instar`; every starbase coordinate should be distinct and
  in range; the ship should not start inside a supernova. No
  extraction needed -- these can be asked of the state directly.
- **Score** (`finish.c:score`). A long tail of `if` and a sum. Pull the
  arithmetic out of the printing and the whole table becomes testable
  from a made-up game.
- **Time and resources** (`events.c`). `d.remtime = d.remres/(d.remkl +
  4*d.remcom)` and the repair loop are small, sharp, and currently
  unchecked in any form.
- **Damage** (`battle.c`). Phaser and torpedo damage, the `fry()`
  device-damage roll, and what shields absorb.
- **Enemy movement** (`ai.c`). Where #42 lives. `movebaddy()` decides a
  direction from forces and distance; that decision is a function of
  numbers and could be asked directly instead of inferred from a
  transcript.

## Acceptance criteria

This is a standing goal rather than one change, so the criteria are for
each slice:

- [ ] A new or extended test binary registered with CTest, following
      the `test_tuifmt` pattern in `CMakeLists.txt`.
- [ ] The extracted function computes and prints nothing.
- [ ] `tests/golden.sh` recordings are unchanged by the extraction --
      if they move, the extraction changed behaviour.
- [ ] Tests state expected values, not merely that a call returns.
- [ ] `ctest --test-dir build` green in Debug and Release.

## Notes

Worth being honest about what this is for. It will not find many bugs
on its own -- the rules are what they are, and a test written from the
code agrees with the code. Its value is that the next change to a rule
has something to argue with, and that the rules stop being knowable
only by reading. #42 is the counter-example that makes the case: a
decades-old defect that survived eight tests, twelve seeded games, a
mutation battery and byte-exact recordings, because none of them knew
what the answer was supposed to be.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

## Verdict: request changes

One comment-only defect, but it is exactly the piece of evidence you asked me to second-opinion, and it is demonstrably wrong. Everything else — the fix, the re-recorded fixture, the battery — checks out and I verified it independently.

Reviewed state: branch `fix/supercommander-diagonal`, working tree on top of `0e3a27e`, uncommitted changes to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/ai.c`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden/combat.txt`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tournament.sh`. No untracked files, no staged/unstaged split.

---

## Findings

### should-fix — `tests/tournament.sh:323-325`: the stated mechanism for the stutter's disappearance is wrong

> `-- he closes on the ship now instead of wandering, so his move is scheduled twice in a pass far less often.`

Both halves are false, and I measured both.

**Scheduling frequency is unchanged.** `events.c:343` sets `future[FSCMOVE] = d.date+0.2777` — a constant period, with no dependence on where the Super-commander is. How many times `FSCMOVE` fires inside one `events()` pass is a function of the elapsed `Time` of the jump and nothing else. I instrumented an `events()` pass counter in two builds (fix applied / fix reverted) and replayed seed 4 on the fight route:

```
=== fixed ===              === bug reverted ===
pass 1 IN 4 5 ent 2 6      pass 1 IN 4 5 ent 2 6
pass 2 IN 3 4 ent 3 7      pass 2 IN 3 4 ent 3 7
pass 3 IN 2 4 ent 2 7      pass 3 IN 2 3 ent 2 7
pass 5 IN 1 4 ent 2 6      pass 5 IN 1 2 ent 2 6
pass 6 IN 1 5 ent 1 6      pass 6 IN 1 2 ent 1 6
pass 6 IN 1 4 ent 1 6      pass 6 IN 1 2 ent 1 6
pass 7 IN 2 3 ent 2 6      pass 7 IN 1 2 ent 2 6
```

Identical pass structure; `FSCMOVE` still fires twice in pass 6 after the fix. The `ai.c:533-541` comment above the guard ("a single warp jump can schedule the Super-commander's move more than once") is still literally true, and the tournament comment now contradicts it.

**He is not closing on the ship.** In every one of those calls he is in the evade branch (`ai.c:385-394`), whose whole purpose is to circulate away. Watch him after the fix: `2 4 → 1 4 → 1 5 → 1 4 → 2 3`. That is wandering, correctly.

**What actually changed** is visible in the right-hand column: with the axis bug he is *frozen* at `1 2` for four consecutive moves. That is the real mechanism, and it follows directly from the typo. When the pursuit vector has `ideltax == 0`, the buggy primary attempt was `iqx = isx+0`, `iqy = isy+0` — his own quadrant — and `checkdest()` (`ai.c:307-311`) accepts it: it rejects only the Enterprise's quadrant, out-of-range, `>899` Klingons, and bases in evade mode. So it performs a no-op move, returns 0, and the fallback manoeuvres never run. Two reports in one pass then name the same quadrant and read as a stutter. With the fix he moves every turn, so the two reports differ and there is no duplicate line for the `awk` to find.

Suggested replacement for lines 320-328:

```
	# Be clear about what this is worth: no seed in the battery
	# currently produces the stutter. Seed 4 did, against a build
	# with that fix reverted, and stopped once the Super-commander's
	# pursuit was corrected -- not because his move is scheduled
	# twice any less often (that is a fixed 0.2777-stardate period,
	# and seed 4 still schedules it twice in one pass), but because
	# the axis bug used to leave him sitting still: with ideltax 0
	# his own quadrant was the destination, checkdest() accepted it,
	# and the two reports in the pass named the same place. Moving
	# every turn, they name different ones. 190 seeds across both
	# routes produced no stutter afterwards. The mechanism is still
	# there, so the check stays; a seed that exercises it again
	# would be worth swapping in.
```

### nit — `tests/tournament.sh:320-321`: "nothing currently to bite on" understates it

The battery still draws four Super-commander reports after the fix (seed 4: 1, seed 21: 1, seed 23: 2), so the `awk` is comparing real report lines, including a seed with two of them in one game. It is an absence check with *input* but no duplicate — worth saying precisely, given how careful the rest of this file is. (Before the fix: six reports, three in seed 4 — the old comment's numbers were right.)

### nit — `tests/tournament.sh:328-329`: the "Back to back" sentence now dangles

It used to follow "so the check has something to bite on"; it now follows "would be worth swapping in" with no blank comment line, and its antecedent is gone. Add a `#` separator before line 329, or move the window explanation up next to line 318.

### nit — `tests/golden.sh:19-21`: stale forward reference

> `and so does the one-character fix to the Super-commander's pursuit in #42`

Written when #42 was pending. Once this lands, it reads as a promise about a change that has already been made. Suggest past tense pointing at the fixture that moved.

---

## Answers to the four things you asked

**1. `ideltay` is genuinely right; it is not a quirk.** The fallback manoeuvres prove it from inside the function. The `ideltax==0 || ideltay==0` branch at `ai.c:472` is labelled "attempt angle move" and, when `ideltax == 0`, varies `iqx` while *reusing* `iqy` from line 469 — it is written on the assumption that line 469 already holds `isy + ideltay`. Under the bug that reuse handed it `isy + 0`, turning the angle move into a pure-x move. Worse, the branch was almost never reached in that case, because the no-op primary attempt succeeded first (see above). The clamps at `ai.c:464-465` also existed only to feed a line that never read the variable. Every reading of the surrounding code says `ideltay`.

**2. One report disappearing is not merely plausible — it is the whole of the available signal, and the fix moved most of it.** I traced the Super-commander through all seven golden journeys: he moves **three times in the entire battery**, all of them in `combat`. Two of those three decisions change:

```
fixed:  4 5 → 3 4 → 2 4 → 1 4
bug:    4 5 → 3 4 → 2 3 → 1 2
```

So the hit rate is 2 of 3, not 1 of many. The output stays otherwise byte-identical for two reasons I confirmed: `scom()` draws exactly one `Rand()` per call on every path through the move cascade, so the generator stays in lockstep and the rest of the galaxy plays identically; and his position reaches the screen only through a 20 %-gated report that is further suppressed by `starch[d.isx][d.isy] > 0`. Instrumenting that decision shows precisely why the line vanished — the corrected Super-commander walks into charted territory:

```
fixed:  REP? pos 2 4 starch 1 irep 0     (suppressed: chart already shows it)
bug:    REP? pos 2 3 starch 0 irep 0     (printed)
```

The same roll passes in both builds. Your instinct that "more should have moved" is right about the *game* and wrong about the *recordings*: the fixtures barely exercise him. If you want the golden battery to be a real net for #42 rather than a four-line tripwire, a journey with `rest` in it would give him a dozen moves instead of three. Not a blocker — I confirmed the current fixture does catch a reintroduction (a reverted build fails `golden.sh` on `combat` and nothing else).

**3. Leave the check where it is; do not delete it and do not chase a replacement seed.** I swept 60 seeds × both routes (120 games) against builds with the #32 guard removed. Fix reverted: exactly one stutter, seed 4 fight. Fix applied: zero, across 31 drawn reports. That reproduces your 190-seed result and confirms the stutter was already a 1-in-120 event before the fix, so "far less often" was never the right frame — the fix removed the only state that produced it. Deleting the check would be wrong (the guard at `ai.c:566` is live code with no other coverage), and hunting a new seed is not worth it when the correct explanation of *why* nothing bites is two sentences. Fix the comment; keep the check. If you ever want it deterministic, the honest form is a unit test that calls `scom()` twice with a stubbed `irep`, not a seed.

**4. The battery's other margins are untouched.** Per-seed contributions to the six aggregate flags are byte-identical between the fixed and reverted builds; only the Super-commander report count differs (6 → 4).

| flag | seeds contributing |
|---|---|
| docked | 7 |
| moved | 10 |
| fought | 12 |
| fired torpedo | 6 |
| impulse hint | 3 (seeds 6, 9, 20) |
| paged | 9 |

Thinnest margin is the impulse hint at 3 of 12, and it is unchanged by this fix. Seed 4 still earns its place in the list on fight/torpedo/page even without the stutter, so keeping it (and its position, which picks the route) is right.

---

## Verified independently

- Clean build with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, zero warnings.
- `ctest --test-dir build`: 9/9 pass.
- `tests/golden.sh` passes against the current tree; against a build with the fix reverted it fails on `combat` only, with exactly the four lines the fixture diff shows.
- `tests/tournament.sh` passes, 12 seeds, Debug, ~59 s.
- CRLF line endings preserved in `ai.c`; `tests/golden/combat.txt` respects the `-text` attribute; no trailing whitespace or over-long lines in the new comment.

## Not reviewed

- TUI behaviour at 80x24 / 72x24 — no code path in this change touches rendering, and no fixture under `tests/tui.sh` mentions the Super-commander.
- The 190-seed claim at full scale; I ran 120 games (seeds 1-60 × both routes) and got a consistent result.

It is an absence check with *input* but no duplicate — worth saying precisely, given how careful the rest of this file is. input.content:
Fixes #42.

```c
iqx = d.isx + ideltax;
iqy = d.isy + ideltax;   /* wants ideltay */
```

It has wanted `ideltay` for as long as this has been C. It is the
Super-commander's *first* choice of move — the fallback manoeuvres below
only run when `checkdest()` turns that one down — so his pursuit has
always been a step along x mirrored onto y.

## What that actually did

The interesting part, which code review worked out by instrumenting both
builds rather than taking my explanation: when the pursuit vector had no
x component, the destination became **his own quadrant**. `checkdest()`
has no objection to that, so the move succeeded by doing nothing and the
fallbacks never ran. He sat still — in one recorded game, for four
consecutive turns.

That is also where the duplicate intelligence report of #32 came from:
two reports in one pass naming the same quadrant, because he had not
left it.

The fallback proves the intent from inside the function. Its "attempt
angle move" branch varies `iqx` and *reuses* `iqy` from the line above,
which is only sensible if that line put `isy + ideltay` there. The clamps
on `ideltay` a few lines up existed to feed a line that never read it.

## Shown, not argued

This is what the golden recordings were landed for. One of the seven
moves — `combat`, by four lines — where a report no longer prints because
the corrected Super-commander walks into charted space and the chart
suppresses it.

I expected more to move and asked review to check that. The answer: he
moves **three times in the whole battery** and **two of those three
decisions change**. `scom()` draws exactly one `Rand()` per call on every
path, so the generator stays in lockstep and the rest of the galaxy plays
identically; his position reaches the screen only through a 20%-gated,
chart-suppressed report. The small diff is the fixtures barely exercising
him, not the fix barely mattering. A journey with `rest` in it would give
him a dozen moves instead of three.

**Plain-mode output changes** for any seeded game he features in, which
is the point.

## Fallout, handled honestly

The battery pinned seed 4 because it reproduced the #32 stutter against a
build with that fix reverted. **It no longer does** — the stutter needed
him frozen. 190 seeds across both routes produce no duplicate now.

The check stays: the guard it covers is live code with no other test. Its
comment now says plainly that nothing currently makes it fail and why —
including a correction to my own first explanation, which claimed his
move is scheduled less often. It isn't; that is a fixed 0.2777-stardate
period and seed 4 still schedules it twice in one pass.

Battery margins are otherwise untouched: docked 7, moved 10, fought 12,
torpedo 6, impulse hint 3, paged 9.

Zero warnings with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`; 9/9 ctest; reverting the fix fails
`golden` on `combat` and nothing else.

Both done. `main` is at `3b893b0`.

**[#50](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/50) filed** — unit-testing the rules. I wrote it around the obstacle rather than the goal, because the obstacle is the whole story: the rules aren't reachable. `battle.c` has 194 calls to `prout`/`scan` woven through its arithmetic, `moving.c` 135, `finish.c` 151 — a function that computes *and* narrates can't be asked a question. The way out is the one `tuifmt.c` already took: `condition_now()` and `sensors_masked()` were extracted precisely so a test could ask them. The issue proposes doing that one rule at a time with the golden recordings as the safety net — if an extraction moves a recording, the extraction changed behaviour and is wrong.

It also says plainly what the work is *not* worth: a test written from the code agrees with the code, so this won't find many bugs on its own. Its value is that the next change to a rule has something to argue with.

**[#42 is fixed](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/pull/51)** — and the golden masters did exactly the job they were built for, one commit after landing. One recording moved, by four lines.

**But my explanation of the bug was wrong, and review proved it with instrumentation rather than argument.** I'd said the Super-commander's move was being scheduled twice per pass less often now. It isn't — that's a fixed 0.2777-stardate period, and the same seed still schedules it twice. What the typo actually did:

> With no x component in the pursuit vector, the destination became **his own quadrant**. `checkdest()` has no objection to that, so the move "succeeded" by doing nothing and the fallbacks never ran. He sat still — four consecutive turns in one recorded game.

Which also explains #32: the duplicate intelligence report was two reports in one pass naming the same quadrant, *because he hadn't left it*. Those two issues were the same bug seen from different ends.

The fallback code proves the intent from inside the function: its "attempt angle move" branch varies `iqx` and **reuses** `iqy` from the buggy line, which only makes sense if that line put `isy + ideltay` there. The clamps on `ideltay` a few lines above existed to feed a line that never read it.

I'd also worried the four-line diff was too small for a fix to his primary movement. Review answered it: he moves **three times in the whole battery, and two of those three decisions change**. The fixtures barely exercise him — a journey with `rest` in it would give him a dozen moves. That's a real coverage gap, noted rather than papered over.

One piece of collateral handled honestly: the battery's stutter check pinned seed 4 because it reproduced #32's bug — which needed him *frozen*. It no longer reproduces, and 190 seeds across both routes produce no duplicate. I kept the check (the guard it covers is live code with no other test) and rewrote its comment to say plainly that nothing currently makes it fail, and why — including correcting my own first explanation in the file itself.

Three issues remain: **#50** (unit tests), **#46** (resize repaint), **#38** (`osx.c` declarations).

content.text:
No — I recommended it and put it top of the list. But my phrasing was worse than too modest; it was wrong in a way worth correcting.

What I wrote — "a test written from the code agrees with the code" — describes a risk in *how you write the tests*, not a limit of the technique. And as filed, #50 invites exactly the weak version: extract a function, run it, paste what it returns, call it an expectation. That would be `golden.sh` with more ceremony, and I already have `golden.sh`.

The strong version derives expectations from `sst.doc`, which is a specification with actual numbers in it:

```
impulse engines require 20 units of energy to engage, plus 10
units per sector (100 units per quadrant) traveled
It costs 50 units of energy to raise shields, nothing to lower them
YELLOW - low on energy (<1000 units)
Ordinary Klingons have about 400 units of energy, Commanders about 1200
```

A test written from those lines is a **second, independent statement of the rules**. When it disagrees with the code, one of the two is wrong and you have to find out which — and either answer is worth having, because a manual that lies is a bug too.

The test of whether this matters is #42. Would a unit test have caught it? **Only in the strong version.** Write the expectation as "the Super-commander closes one quadrant on each axis toward his target" and it fails on the first assertion. Run `supercommander()` and record where he actually went, and you enshrine the bug for another decade — which is precisely what the golden recordings would have done had they existed in 1995.

So the honest ordering is: the rules that `sst.doc` states in numbers are worth testing and can genuinely find bugs; the rules it doesn't state (enemy movement heuristics, the score weights) can only be characterized, and `golden.sh` already does that more cheaply. The issue should say which category each of its five proposed slices falls into, and it currently doesn't.

Want me to rewrite #50 along those lines? It'd be a better issue for it, and it changes what "done" means for the first slice.

input.content:
## Goal

Test the game's rules against an independent statement of what they
are, so that when the code and the statement disagree, somebody finds
out.

## The rule that makes this worth doing

**An expected value is derived from `sst.doc`. It is never obtained by
running the code and writing down what came out.**

That single distinction is the whole issue. A test whose expectation
was copied from current behaviour is `tests/golden.sh` with more
ceremony, and `golden.sh` already does that job byte for byte across
seven journeys, more cheaply and more thoroughly than a unit test will.
Writing more of those adds work and finds nothing.

A test whose expectation was derived from the manual is a *second
opinion*. When it disagrees with the code, one of the two is wrong and
somebody has to decide which -- and either answer is worth having,
because a manual that lies is a defect too.

This is test-driven development applied to code that already exists.
The reason TDD finds bugs is not the ordering ritual; it is that the
expectation is written before there is an implementation to copy it
from. Thirty-year-old code cannot be written test-first, but the manual
can play the part the not-yet-written code would have played.

## What that would have been worth

#42: the Super-commander added his x delta to both axes, so whenever
his pursuit had no x component he "moved" to the quadrant he was
already in, `checkdest()` accepted it, and he sat still. Decades.

- Expectation derived from intent -- *he closes one quadrant on each
  axis toward his target* -- fails on the first assertion.
- Expectation obtained by running `supercommander()` and recording
  where he went -- passes forever, and enshrines the bug.

Eight tests, twelve seeded games, a mutation battery and byte-exact
recordings all held the second kind of answer. It took someone reading
the line.

## What can be tested this way, and what cannot

The manual specifies some rules in numbers and is silent on others.
Only the first kind gets a real test; for the second, `golden.sh`
already records what happens and a unit test would add nothing.

**Specified -- worth testing, in roughly this order:**

- **Score** (`finish.c:score`, spec at `sst.doc:1355-1378`). Fifteen
  rules with exact values: 10 a Klingon, 50 a commander, 200 the
  Super-commander, 3 a capture, 20 a Romulan destroyed, 1 surrendered,
  500 times the kill rate, a win bonus of 100 per skill grade; less
  200 for dying, 100 a starbase, 100 a ship, 100 an Algeron violation,
  45 a call for help, 10 a planet, 5 a star, 1 a casualty. The
  arithmetic is one expression, the printing is around it, and a
  reading suggests they agree -- which is worth *proving* rather than
  assuming, and worth having pinned afterwards.
- **Impulse and shields energy** (`moving.c`, `battle.c`, spec at
  `sst.doc:626-627,646,660`). 20 units to engage impulse plus 10 a
  sector; 50 to raise shields; 200 to activate high-speed shield
  control. Small, sharp, and checkable from a made-up ship.
- **Condition thresholds** (`tuifmt.c:condition_now`, spec at
  `sst.doc:376`). Yellow below 1000 units. Already extracted and
  already tested -- listed to show the shape the others should take.
- **Warp movement and time** (`moving.c`, spec at `sst.doc:572,620`).
  Warp damaged under 10 stardates still allows warp 4; impulse moves
  at 0.95 sectors per stardate.
- **Galaxy invariants** (`setup.c`). Not prose in the manual, but they
  follow from what `d.galaxy` means: the Klingons, starbases and stars
  it encodes must sum to `inkling`, `inbase`, `instar`; base
  coordinates must be distinct and in range. Checkable from the state
  with no extraction at all -- the cheapest place to start.

**Unspecified -- do not write unit tests for these:**

- Enemy movement heuristics (`ai.c:movebaddy`), the forces calculation,
  the retreat thresholds. The manual describes them in words only, and
  a test would just restate the code.
- Damage-roll distributions, event scheduling intervals.

`golden.sh` covers the second group as characterization. If one of them
needs pinning harder, add a journey there rather than a unit test.

## The obstacle, and the way round it

The rules are not reachable on their own. Two problems, both of which
the codebase already shows the way past:

1. **Global state.** ~90 globals declared through the
   `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`, so a test has to compose a
   whole game before asking a question. `tests/test_tuifmt.c` already
   does this: it defines `INCLUDED`, includes `sst.h`, and has a
   `basestate()` that sets up a plausible ship and quadrant.

2. **Arithmetic tangled with output.** `battle.c` has 194 calls to
   `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`scan` woven through its sums, `moving.c`
   135, `finish.c` 151. A function that computes *and* narrates cannot
   be asked a question without capturing its narration.

   The way out is the one `tuifmt.c` took: pull the decision into a
   function that computes and says nothing, leave the narration where
   it was. `condition_now()` and `sensors_masked()` are both exactly
   that, with comments saying why.

## Suggested approach

One rule at a time, each with the golden recordings as the safety net:
extract the pure function, confirm the recordings do not move, then
write the test from the manual. If a recording *does* move, the
extraction changed behaviour and is wrong.

Start with the galaxy invariants (no extraction needed) and the score
(one expression, a complete spec).

## Acceptance criteria

Per slice, not for the issue as a whole:

- [ ] Every expected value cites the `sst.doc` line it came from, in a
      comment, or is explicitly marked as a characterization with a
      reason it could not be derived.
- [ ] No expectation was obtained by running the code.
- [ ] The extracted function computes and prints nothing.
- [ ] `tests/golden.sh` recordings are unchanged by the extraction.
- [ ] A new or extended test binary registered with CTest, following
      the `test_tuifmt` pattern in `CMakeLists.txt`.
- [ ] `ctest --test-dir build` green in Debug and Release.

## Notes

If a test derived from the manual fails, that is a finding, not a
broken test. Work out whether the code or the manual is wrong before
changing either -- and if it is the manual, say so in the commit, since
`sst.doc` is the only specification this game has.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

  reading suggests they agree -- which is worth *proving* rather than
  assuming, and worth having pinned afterwards.
- **Impulse and shields energy** (`moving.c`, `battle.c`, spec at
  `sst.doc:626-627,646,660`). 20 units to engage impulse plus 10 a
  sector; 50 to raise shields; 200 to activate high-speed shield
  control. Small, sharp, and checkable from a made-up ship.
- **Condition thresholds** (`tuifmt.c:condition_now`, spec at
  `sst.doc:376`). Yellow below 1000 units. Already extracted and
  already tested -- listed to show the shape the others should take.
- **Warp movement and time** (`moving.c`, spec at `sst.doc:572,620`).
  Warp damaged under 10 stardates still allows warp 4; impulse moves
  at 0.95 sectors per stardate.
- **Galaxy invariants** (`setup.c`). Not prose in the manual, but they
  follow from what `d.galaxy` means: the Klingons, starbases and stars
  it encodes must sum to `inkling`, `inbase`, `instar`; base
  coordinates must be distinct and in range. Checkable from the state
  with no extraction at all -- the cheapest place to start.

**Unspecified -- do not write unit tests for these:**

- Enemy movement heuristics (`ai.c:movebaddy`), the forces calculation,
  the retreat thresholds. The manual describes them in words only, and
  a test would just restate the code.
- Damage-roll distributions, event scheduling intervals.

`golden.sh` covers the second group as characterization. If one of them
needs pinning harder, add a journey there rather than a unit test.

## The obstacle, and the way round it

The rules are not reachable on their own. Two problems, both of which
the codebase already shows the way past:

1. **Global state.** ~90 globals declared through the
   `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`, so a test has to compose a
   whole game before asking a question. `tests/test_tuifmt.c` already
   does this: it defines `INCLUDED`, includes `sst.h`, and has a
   `basestate()` that sets up a plausible ship and quadrant.

2. **Arithmetic tangled with output.** `battle.c` has 194 calls to
   `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`scan` woven through its sums, `moving.c`
   135, `finish.c` 151. A function that computes *and* narrates cannot
   be asked a question without capturing its narration.

   The way out is the one `tuifmt.c` took: pull the decision into a
   function that computes and says nothing, leave the narration where
   it was. `condition_now()` and `sensors_masked()` are both exactly
   that, with comments saying why.

## Suggested approach

One rule at a time, each with the golden recordings as the safety net:
extract the pure function, confirm the recordings do not move, then
write the test from the manual. If a recording *does* move, the
extraction changed behaviour and is wrong.

Start with the galaxy invariants (no extraction needed) and the score
(one expression, a complete spec).

## Acceptance criteria

Per slice, not for the issue as a whole:

- [ ] Every expected value cites the `sst.doc` line it came from, in a
      comment, or is explicitly marked as a characterization with a
      reason it could not be derived.
- [ ] No expectation was obtained by running the code.
- [ ] The extracted function computes and prints nothing.
- [ ] `tests/golden.sh` recordings are unchanged by the extraction.
- [ ] A new or extended test binary registered with CTest, following
      the `test_tuifmt` pattern in `CMakeLists.txt`.
- [ ] `ctest --test-dir build` green in Debug and Release.

## Notes

If a test derived from the manual fails, that is a finding, not a
broken test. Work out whether the code or the manual is wrong before
changing either -- and if it is the manual, say so in the commit, since
`sst.doc` is the only specification this game has.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

[#50 rewritten](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/50), retitled **"Test the game's rules against sst.doc, not against its own output"**, with one rule at the top:

> An expected value is derived from `sst.doc`. It is never obtained by running the code and writing down what came out.

Your framing is the right one and I've put it in the issue: TDD doesn't find bugs because of the ordering ritual, it finds them because **the expectation is written before there's an implementation to copy it from**. Thirty-year-old code can't be written test-first — but the manual can play the part the not-yet-written code would have played.

#42 is the worked example, and it's stark:

- expectation from intent — *he closes one quadrant on each axis toward his target* — fails on the first assertion
- expectation from running `supercommander()` — passes forever, and enshrines the bug

The issue now splits the work by whether an oracle actually exists, because that's what decides if a test is worth writing:

**Specified, worth testing.** Score is the strongest — `sst.doc:1355-1378` gives fifteen rules with exact values, and `finish.c` computes them in one expression. Also impulse and shield energy costs (20 to engage plus 10 a sector, 50 to raise shields, 200 for high-speed control), the yellow-condition threshold, warp/impulse timing. Plus galaxy invariants, which aren't prose but follow from what `d.galaxy` encodes and need no extraction at all — the cheapest place to start.

**Unspecified, don't.** Enemy movement heuristics, forces calculations, damage-roll distributions. The manual describes them in words only, so a unit test would just restate the code. `golden.sh` already characterizes them, more cheaply.

That distinction is the part I got wrong first time. Writing the weak kind of test isn't merely low-value — it's actively worse than nothing, because it looks like verification while being a second copy of the implementation.

One thing I'll flag honestly: reading `finish.c`'s scoring expression against the manual, **they appear to agree** — all fifteen coefficients line up. So the first slice will probably pass. That's still worth doing: it proves the manual is a usable oracle rather than a lie, and pins the arithmetic afterwards. But nobody should expect a bug harvest from slice one.

The acceptance criteria now require every expected value to cite the `sst.doc` line it came from, or be explicitly marked as characterization with a reason — and the closing note says that a failing test derived from the manual is a *finding*, not a broken test: decide whether the code or the manual is wrong before changing either.

/* Rules the manual states in numbers.
 *
 * Everything here computes and narrates nothing, so it can be asked a
 * question directly -- which is the point. tests/test_rules.c checks
 * these against sst.doc rather than against what the code happens to
 * return, so that when the two disagree somebody finds out.
 */
#ifndef SST_RULES_H
#define SST_RULES_H

/* The parts of the score sheet that are worked out rather than simply
 * counted. The per-line points -- ten a Klingon, fifty a commander --
 * are multiplications the sheet does as it prints them; what needs
 * computing is the kill rate, the bonus, how many ships were lost, who
 * surrendered, and the sum of the lot.
 *
 * Spec: sst.doc, "Scoring is fairly simple", lines 1352-1378.
 */
struct scoring {
	double perdate;		/* Klingon kills per stardate */
	int killrate;		/* 500 times that, rounded */
	int winbonus;		/* 100 a skill grade, if the game was won */
	int shipslost;		/* 0 the Enterprise, 1 the Faerie Queene, 2 both */
	int surrendered;	/* Romulans who gave up; only counts on a win */
	int total;		/* the number at the foot of the sheet */
};

/* inGame is true for the SCORE command, which reports a game still
 * being played; false when the game has ended. elapsed is the
 * stardates the game has run, before the minimum the manual applies. */
void score_compute(struct scoring *s, int inGame, double elapsed);

#endif	/* SST_RULES_H */

content.text:
## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `test/rules-from-the-manual` at HEAD `3b893b0` (identical to `main`) plus the uncommitted worktree: modified `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakeLists.txt` and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/finish.c`; new `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/rules.c`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/rules.h`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/test_rules.c`. Nothing staged; no stray files (the CI/AGENTS/tui.sh entries in the session's opening snapshot are no longer present).

The extraction itself is clean and I have stronger evidence than `golden.sh` for it (below). The changes I'm asking for are in the tests: three of the fifteen rules are not actually pinned, and one comment misreads its own condition.

### What I verified independently

I built the old `score()` arithmetic verbatim from `main`'s `finish.c` alongside `score_compute()` and ran 2,000,000 randomised states through both — covering `elapsed == 0`, sub-5-stardate, and long games; both `inGame` values; all three `ship` values; `gamewon` both ways; `alive` both ways. **Zero mismatches** on all six outputs (`perdate`, `killrate`, `winbonus`, `shipslost`, `surrendered`, `total`). The extraction is behaviour-preserving.

Answering your three specific worries:

- **`timused` clamp**: safe. In `main` it was a function-local `double`, never written back to anything, so pulling it into `score_compute` is invisible. Confirmed by the differential.
- **`perdate`**: still written back at `finish.c:344`, and both consumers (`finish.c:370`, `plaque()` at `finish.c:480`) read the global. Unchanged.
- **`iskill`**: untouched at `finish.c:342`, still set before anything can read it; `plaque()` at `finish.c:470` is the only consumer.
- **One thing you moved that you didn't mention**: `main` read `d.date - indate` and `d.nromrem` *before* `pause(0)`; the new code reads them after. `pause()` (`sst.c:769`) only prints and calls `getch()`, so this is safe — but it is a real reordering, worth knowing you made.
- **Where `golden.sh` does not cover you**: no fixture reaches a won game. `grep` for "Bonus for winning" across `tests/golden/` finds nothing, so the win bonus, the Romulan-surrender line, and `klship == 2` are outside the recordings entirely. `golden.sh` being unchanged is real but partial evidence; the differential is what actually covers those branches.

**`nothing_happened()` leaves nothing relevant uninitialised.** Everything `score_compute` reads outside `d` lives in the file-scope struct `a` (`ship`, `skill`, `gamewon`, `alive`, `casual`, `nhelp`, `ncviol` — see `sst.h:179-246`), which is zero-initialised at program start, and every field is explicitly reset per test. One thing to know: `kcaptured` is `#define kcaptured d.kcaptured` (`sst.h:227`), not a separate global, so `test_rules.c:46` is redundant with the `memset` — harmless, but it isn't doing what it looks like it's doing.

**The isolation trick is sound**, and I confirmed it doesn't hide anything: I mutated every coefficient, both `shipslost` branches, both `surrendered` conditions, the death penalty, the floor constant, and the `perdate` divisor — all killed. The trick's bound is that `killrate` stays 0 only while total kills < 100 at 100000 stardates; every fixture is far under. See nit 5 for making that bound self-checking rather than assumed.

### Findings

**1. should-fix — `rules.c:42` / `tests/test_rules.c:97-117`: rule (6)'s contribution to the total is unverified.**
Mutating `+ s->surrendered` to `+ 0*s->surrendered` **survives the whole suite** (I ran it). `test_score_surrender` asserts only `s.surrendered`; no test ever puts a surrender into `s.total`, and `test_score_adds_up` doesn't include one. The comment at `test_rules.c:64-67` claims to cover `sst.doc:1362` under gains, but the gains tests never set `d.nromrem`.
Fix: in the winning case at `test_rules.c:105-109`, add `checkint("...and a point each on the sheet", s.total, 106);` — 6 for the surrenders plus the 100 Novice win bonus that `gamewon = 1` brings with it (verified).

**2. should-fix — `rules.c:44` / `tests/test_rules.c:224-230`: rule (8)'s bonus never reaches an asserted total.**
Mutating `+ s->winbonus` to `+ 0*s->winbonus` **survives**. The rating loop checks `s.winbonus` but never `s.total`, so a bonus that is computed correctly and then dropped from the sum passes.
Fix: add `checkint("and the bonus is in the score", s.total, want[i]);` inside the loop — with `nothing_happened()` and `elapsed = 10.0` the total is exactly the bonus (verified: SGOOD → 300).

**3. should-fix — `rules.c:18` / `tests/test_rules.c:201-207`: the manual's "if you lose the game" qualifier on the floor is untested in the negative.**
Mutating the condition to `if ((1) && elapsed < 5.0)` — i.e. making the 5-stardate floor unconditional — **survives**. The floor test only exercises `d.remkl = 1`; nothing asserts that a *won* short game keeps its real rate, which is the whole content of `sst.doc:1363-1365`. This is the one place a manual-derived suite ought to be strictly better than `golden.sh`, and right now it isn't.
Fix: add a case with `gamewon = 1; d.remkl = 0; d.killk = 2;` and `score_compute(&s, FALSE, 1.0)`, asserting `s.killrate == 1000` (two kills in one stardate, no floor — verified).

**4. should-fix — `rules.c:15-17`: the comment mislabels the condition it explains.**
"The first half of the test is the game not being over" — the first half is `elapsed == 0`; the game-not-over test is the *second* disjunct, `d.remkl != 0`. And the `elapsed == 0` guard's actual job, keeping the division on line 19 away from zero when a game ends on its start date, goes unexplained. In a file whose stated value is that every line points at the manual, a comment pointing at the wrong clause is the defect. Fix: name the two disjuncts separately — `d.remkl != 0` is the manual's "if you lose the game", `elapsed == 0` is the divide-by-zero guard the manual says nothing about.

**5. nit — `tests/test_rules.c:34-35`: dead fixture state.**
`nothing_happened()` sets `d.date` and `indate`, which `score_compute` never reads — elapsed time is a parameter. Harmless today, but it implies the fixture controls game length, so the next person to add a rate test may set `d.date` and be puzzled. Drop both lines, or say in the comment that elapsed time is passed in.

Nothing in the suite said what an answer *should* be. `golden.sh` records
what the game printed last time, `tournament.sh` asks whether things
happened, and neither can tell a right number from a wrong one that has
been wrong for thirty years — which is how the Super-commander (#42) came
to chase along one axis with all of it watching.

values. That makes it an oracle rather than prose.

`score()`'s arithmetic moves to `rules.c`, which computes and narrates
nothing — the pattern `tuifmt.c` already set for the panels. The printing
stays where it was and reads its numbers from a small struct. Nothing a
player sees changes, and the recordings say so.

`tests/test_rules.c` asks that arithmetic what the manual's rules add up
to, every expectation carrying the line it came from. **The rule for this
file and the ones that follow it: an expectation is derived from the
manual, never obtained by running the code.** A test written the other way
agrees with the code by construction, and `golden.sh` already does that
job for a tenth of the effort.

## It earned its keep before it was finished

My first draft scored a game of three Klingons at 30. The code answered
180 — because kills pay twice, once as kills and once through rule (7),
the kill rate, and I had not read that far. **The manual was right and I
was wrong**, which is exactly the argument this kind of test exists to
have. The comment in the test records the mistake, because the next
person will make it too.

Three rules my tests did not actually pin. Zeroing the surrender term,
zeroing the win bonus, or making the five-stardate floor unconditional
**all passed the suite**:

- surrender and bonus were asserted on their own but never on the total,
  so a value computed correctly and then dropped from the sum went
  unnoticed;
- the floor had no case for a game that was *won* short — which is the
  entire content of "**if you lose the game**, your kill rate is based on
  a minimum of 5 stardates".

All three now fail when mutated, along with every coefficient, the death
penalty and the rounding.

Stronger than the recordings: review ran **two million randomised states**
through the old arithmetic and the new side by side — covering
`elapsed == 0`, sub-5-stardate and long games, both `inGame` values, all
three ship states, won and lost, alive and dead — with **no mismatch on
any of the six outputs**.

That matters because no golden fixture reaches a won game, so the win
bonus, the surrender line and losing both ships were outside `golden.sh`'s
reach entirely. `golden OK` was real but partial evidence, and I would
have over-trusted it.

just as completely, and is the obvious next slice.

	   game rounds the whole thing away rather than scaling it.

	   company. The manual says "points in penalties", and the score
	   sheet lists eight kinds; this counts six of them. Losing your
	   ship is folded in below. The death penalty is moot -- a dead
	   captain is not promoted -- but a Treaty of Algeron violation
	   costs a hundred points and does not raise this bar at all. See
	   the note in tests/test_rules.c. */
	p->penalties = 5.0*d.starkl		/* sst.doc:1377 */
		     + casual			/* sst.doc:1378 */
		     + 10.0*d.nplankl		/* sst.doc:1376 */
		     + 45.0*nhelp		/* sst.doc:1375 */

	   its size is the code's own, the manual only says it rises. */
	p->needed = 0.1*skill*(skill + 1.0) + 0.1 + 0.008*p->penalties;

	p->achieved = elapsed < 5.0 ? 0.0

The extraction is behaviour-preserving — verified, not just read.** The penalty terms are summed in the same order (FP addition is not associative, so that matters and you kept it), the threshold expression is character-for-character the original, and `achieved = elapsed < 5.0 ? 0.0 : kills/elapsed` combined with `earned = elapsed < 5.0 || achieved >= needed` reproduces the short-circuit exactly: the division still never runs below five stardates, and the comparison's sense is unchanged. I ran a differential harness (old inline `badpt` block from `finish.c` verbatim vs. `promotion_compute`) over 2,000,000 randomized states covering all three `ship` values, all five skills, and elapsed values straddling 5.0 including 0.0: **0 mismatches**. The one theoretical difference — storing `achieved`/`needed` in `double` struct members forces a round to `double` where the original could have compared at extended precision — only bites on `FLT_EVAL_METHOD == 2` targets (32-bit x87), and the golden test would surface it there. Not worth code changes.

**2. The tests are genuinely derived from `sst.doc:1380-1387`, and the rule is read correctly.** `0.1*skill*(skill+1.0)+0.1` for `skill` 1..5 is 0.3/0.7/1.3/2.1/3.1, which matches `want[]`; `SNOVICE=1 … SEMERITUS=5` (`sst.h:305`) matches the manual's "skill ranges from 1 for Novice to 5 for Emeritus". The 99-vs-100 pair pins the manual's "100 or more" as a strict floor from both sides (`d.basekl = 1` → exactly 100 is *not* zeroed, so a `<` → `<=` mutation dies). The `100.0*d.basekl` → `sst.doc:1372` etc. citations all check out against the loss list. The `promotion_compute` comment's "eight kinds, this counts six" is accurate (missing: death 1371, Algeron 1374).

**3. The boundary call is right, and there is no defect hiding there.** The bar for Novice evaluates to `0.30000000000000004` (0.1 → 0.2 is an exact doubling, then `+0.1` rounds up two ulps), while `3.0/10.0` rounds to `0.29999999999999999`. There is no cheap re-association that fixes it — `0.1*(skill*(skill+1.0)+1.0)` gives the same `0.30000000000000004`. And the manual states the bar without saying what happens to a captain who lands precisely on it, so `>=` vs `>` is unspecified: the `>=` → `>` mutation survives your suite, correctly. Moving the cases off the boundary and recording why in a comment is the right call.

**#53 is correctly scoped out.** Counting `ncviol` changes who gets promoted — a gameplay change, not an extraction — and it is recorded in both `rules.c` and the test file. Keep it out.

**should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/test_rules.c:339-345`** ("commanders count towards the rate"). This case is the one you moved everything else off: `d.killc = 3; d.nsckill = 1` gives 0.4, but its power to detect a dropped term rests on the boundary. I mutated `promotion_compute` to drop `d.nsckill` from the sum; the test does fail — with `achieved = 3/10 = 0.29999999999999999` against a bar of `0.30000000000000004`, i.e. it fails by 1 ulp, for the exact reason your comment three lines below says the tests avoid. Re-associate the bar's formula or add an epsilon anywhere and this case silently stops proving that `nsckill` counts. Fix: `d.killc = 2; d.nsckill = 2;` — still 0.4, and dropping either term gives an unambiguous 0.2 < 0.3. (Verified: kills the mutant robustly.)

**should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/rules.c:91`.** The `0.008` penalty scale factor is not pinned by any test: I mutated it to `0.08` and the full suite passes. Only the degenerate `0.008` → `0.0` mutation is caught (by `checkint("which raises the bar", p.needed > 0.3, 1)`), so the verification claim that "the penalty scale factor" mutation fails a test isn't quite true. The factor isn't in the manual, so no doc-derived expectation can cover it — but this file already accepts characterization tests for undocumented behaviour (`test_promotion_short_game`), and consistency argues for one assertion in the same spirit: with `d.basekl = 1` (100 points), `checkrate("... not in the manual: the code scales by 0.008", p.needed, 1.1)`.

**nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/test_rules.c:432-443`** (`test_promotion_short_game`). Nothing checks `p.achieved` on a short game, though `rules.h:42-43` documents it as 0. I mutated away just the `elapsed < 5.0 ? 0.0 :` guard on `achieved` (leaving `earned`'s): the suite passes while `promotion_compute(&p, 0.0)` now returns `achieved = 0.0/0.0 = NaN` to any future caller. One line fixes it: `checkrate("and is not asked for a rate", p.achieved, 0.0);`.

**nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/test_rules.c:24-29`.** `checkrate` is NaN-blind: for `got = NaN` both `got - want > 1e-6` and `want - got > 1e-6` are false, so the check passes vacuously — which is what let the mutant above through. Invert the sense so NaN fails:

```c
if (!(got - want <= 1e-6 && want - got <= 1e-6)) {
```

The 1e-6 tolerance itself is right: the largest quantity compared is 200.0, where double round-off is ~1e-14, so it is roughly eight orders of magnitude looser than the noise and eight orders tighter than any rule distinction (the smallest gap the tests rely on is 0.3 vs 0.4).

input.content:
test: check the promotion rule against the manual, and find a gap

sst.doc says what Starfleet asks before it promotes a captain: a kill
rate of 0.1 * skill * (skill + 1) + 0.1, raised if a hundred or more
points have been lost in penalties. The code said the same thing inside
finish.c, in the middle of the prose that announces the promotion,
where nothing could ask it a question.

So promotion_compute joins score_compute in rules.c, and the tests ask
it what the manual requires: the bar at each of the five ratings, the
kill rate earning it, the hundred-point floor from both sides, and each
penalty counted at the rate the score sheet gives it.

The gap it found is #53. The manual raises the bar for "points lost in
penalties" and lists eight kinds; this counts six. One of the two is
the death penalty, which is moot -- a dead captain is not promoted. The
other is the Treaty of Algeron, so a captain can cloak in the Neutral
Zone three times, lose three hundred points for it on the score sheet,
and still be promoted on the kill rate a spotless captain needs. Almost
certainly age: this arithmetic predates cloaking. Left alone here,
because changing it changes who gets promoted and that is its own
slice; the code says so where it happens.

One expectation had to be withdrawn rather than kept. Three kills in
ten stardates is a rate of 0.3 and the Novice bar is 0.3, so it should
earn a promotion and does not: the bar comes to 0.30000000000000004 in
binary and three tenths comes to a hair under. The manual states the
bar and says nothing about a captain landing exactly on it, so neither
does the test -- the cases sit either side, and a comment says why.

Review then found the tests softer than they looked in four places: the
case proving super-commanders count towards the rate only did so by one
ulp, the penalty scale factor was pinned by nothing, a short game's
unused rate could quietly become a NaN, and the comparison helper would
have let that NaN pass. All four now fail when mutated.

Behaviour is unchanged, and by more than the recordings say: review ran
two million random states through the old inline arithmetic and the new
side by side with no mismatch, including the short-circuit that keeps
the division away from a game no stardates long.

Part of #50.

input.content:
Second slice of #50.

`sst.doc:1380-1387` says what Starfleet asks before it promotes a
captain: a kill rate of `0.1 * skill * (skill + 1) + 0.1`, raised if a
hundred or more points have been lost in penalties. The code said the
same thing inside `finish.c`, in the middle of the prose announcing the
promotion, where nothing could ask it a question.

`promotion_compute()` joins `score_compute()` in `rules.c`, and the tests
ask it what the manual requires: the bar at each of the five ratings, the
kill rate that earns it, the hundred-point floor from both sides, and
each penalty counted at the rate the score sheet gives it.

## It found something: #53

The manual raises the bar for "points lost in penalties" and lists eight
kinds. **This counts six.**

One absentee is the death penalty, which is moot — a dead captain is not
promoted. The other is the **Treaty of Algeron**, so a captain can cloak
in the Neutral Zone three times, lose 300 points for it on the score
sheet, and still be promoted on the kill rate a spotless captain needs.

Almost certainly age: this arithmetic predates cloaking, which arrived
behind `#ifdef CLOAKING` and added a penalty to the score sheet without
adding it here.

**Left alone in this PR** — changing it changes who gets promoted, which
is a gameplay change and its own slice. Filed as #53, and the code says
so where it happens.

## One expectation withdrawn

Three kills in ten stardates is a rate of 0.3, and the Novice bar is 0.3,
so it should earn a promotion. It doesn't: the bar comes to
`0.30000000000000004` in binary and three tenths to a hair under.

I concluded the *test* was over-specified rather than the game wrong —
the manual states the bar and says nothing about a captain landing
exactly on it. Review agreed and checked there was no defect hiding
behind it (no re-association fixes it; `>=` vs `>` is genuinely
unspecified). The cases now sit either side of the bar, with a comment
saying why.

## What review caught

Four places where the tests were softer than they looked:

- the case proving Super-Commanders count towards the kill rate **only
  did so by one ulp** — the very boundary the comment three lines below
  says the tests avoid;
- the `0.008` penalty scale factor was **pinned by nothing** (I claimed
  it was; only the degenerate mutation to `0.0` died);
- a short game's unused rate could quietly become **NaN**;
- and `checkrate` was **NaN-blind**, which is what let that through.

All four now fail when mutated.

## Evidence

Behaviour unchanged, by more than the recordings: review ran **two
million randomised states** through the old inline `badpt` block and the
new function side by side — all three ship values, all five skills,
elapsed straddling 5.0 including 0.0 — with no mismatch, including the
short-circuit that keeps the division away from a game no stardates long.

10/10 ctest; zero warnings with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`; `golden.sh` unchanged.

**This slice found a real one.** `sst.doc` raises the promotion bar for "100 or more points in penalties" and lists eight kinds of penalty. The code counts six. One absentee is the death penalty, which is moot — a dead captain isn't promoted. The other is the **Treaty of Algeron**: a captain can cloak in the Neutral Zone three times, lose 300 points for it on the score sheet, and still be promoted on exactly the kill rate a spotless captain needs.

Almost certainly age — that arithmetic predates cloaking, which arrived behind `#ifdef CLOAKING` and added a penalty to the score sheet without adding it here. Filed as **[#53](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/53)** and left alone: it changes who gets promoted, so it's a gameplay change and its own slice.

That's the first thing #50 has turned up in the game rather than in my own tests, and it's the exact shape the issue predicted — a rule stated in the manual, implemented six-eighths.

**One expectation I had to withdraw.** Three kills in ten stardates is a rate of 0.3 and the Novice bar is 0.3, so it should earn promotion. It doesn't: the bar comes to `0.30000000000000004` in binary, three tenths to a hair under. I judged the *test* over-specified rather than the game wrong — the manual states the bar and says nothing about landing precisely on it. Review checked that independently before agreeing: no re-association fixes it, and `>=` versus `>` is genuinely unspecified. The cases now sit either side.

**Review also found four places my tests were softer than they looked**, and one of them corrects something I told you:

- the case proving Super-Commanders count toward the kill rate only did so **by one ulp** — sitting on the very boundary the comment three lines below says the tests avoid;
- the `0.008` penalty scale factor was **pinned by nothing**. I'd claimed it was covered; only the degenerate mutation to `0.0` died;
- a short game's unused rate could quietly become **NaN**;
- and `checkrate` was **NaN-blind**, which is what let that through — a comparison written so that `NaN` passes everything.

All four now fail under mutation. That last pair is worth noting as a pattern: the helper that checks the answers was itself the weakest link, and no amount of careful expectation-writing would have surfaced it.

The extraction is behaviour-preserving on stronger evidence than the recordings again — two million randomised states through the old inline `badpt` block and the new function, no mismatch, including the short-circuit that keeps the division away from a game no stardates long.

**Remaining:** #53 (the Algeron gap — the natural next thing, now that the test is there waiting for it), #50 (more slices: impulse and shield energy costs are next in the specified list), #46 (resize repaint), #38 (`osx.c` declarations).

void promotion_compute(struct promotion *p, double elapsed)
{
	/* "if you have lost 100 or more points in penalties, the required
	   kill rate goes up" -- sst.doc:1383-1385. Below a hundred the
	   game rounds the whole thing away rather than scaling it.

	   Which penalties count is where the code and the manual part
	   company. The manual says "points in penalties", and the score
	   sheet lists eight kinds; this counts six of them. Losing your
	   ship is folded in below. The death penalty is moot -- a dead
	   captain is not promoted -- but a Treaty of Algeron violation
	   costs a hundred points and does not raise this bar at all. See
	   the note in tests/test_rules.c. */
	p->penalties = 5.0*d.starkl		/* sst.doc:1377 */
		     + casual			/* sst.doc:1378 */
		     + 10.0*d.nplankl		/* sst.doc:1376 */
		     + 45.0*nhelp		/* sst.doc:1375 */
		     + 100.0*d.basekl;		/* sst.doc:1372 */
	if (ship == IHF) p->penalties += 100.0;		/* sst.doc:1373 */
	else if (ship == 0) p->penalties += 200.0;
	if (p->penalties < 100.0) p->penalties = 0.0;

	/* "Normally, the required kill rate is 0.1 * skill * (skill + 1.0)
	   + 0.1, where skill ranges from 1 for Novice to 5 for Emeritus."
	   -- sst.doc:1385-1387. The penalty term is the "goes up" part;
	   its size is the code's own, the manual only says it rises. */
	p->needed = 0.1*skill*(skill + 1.0) + 0.1 + 0.008*p->penalties;

	/* A game won in under five stardates is promoted without being
	   asked for a rate -- which the manual does not mention, and
	   which the division below could not survive anyway when a game
	   is won on the stardate it began. */
	p->achieved = elapsed < 5.0 ? 0.0
		    : (d.killk + d.killc + d.nsckill)/elapsed;

## Verdict: request changes

One small, concrete test gap. The production change itself is correct and I'd approve it as written; the branch is a test-driven slice, and the property the change is *about* (the term sits inside the floor's reach) survives mutation untested.

Reviewed state: branch `fix/algeron-raises-promotion-bar` at `bfe7726` plus the two-file unstaged working-tree diff (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/rules.c`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/test_rules.c`). Nothing staged, nothing untracked. I built with `-DSST_WERROR=ON` (clean), ran all 10 ctest targets (pass), and compiled both `rules.c` and `test_rules.c` with `CLOAKING` undefined (clean, tests pass).

## Findings

### should-fix — `tests/test_rules.c:387-405`: nothing tests that the term is inside the floor's reach

You asked specifically whether the placement before the 100-point clamp is right. It is, but no test can tell. I moved the whole `#ifdef CLOAKING` block to *after* `if (p->penalties < 100.0) p->penalties = 0.0;` and the entire suite still reports "All tests passed" — because every new case has `ncviol >= 1`, which clears the floor on its own either way.

Failure scenario the current tests miss: 99 points of other penalty plus one violation. Correct behaviour is 199 (the violation carries the rest over the floor, and all of it counts). With the term after the clamp it is 100 — the ninety-nine silently vanish, and a captain who called for help twice and took nine casualties gets a bar 0.792 lower than the manual's rule gives them.

Suggested addition, next to the existing floor test:

```c
	/* Ninety-nine points is under the floor on its own; a violation
	   carries the rest of them over it, and then all of it counts. */
	nothing_happened();
	skill = SNOVICE;
	nhelp = 2;		/*  90 */
	casual = 9;		/*   9 */
	ncviol = 1;		/* 100 */
	promotion_compute(&p, 10.0);
	checkrate("a violation carries the rest over the floor",
		  p.penalties, 199.0);
```

I confirmed this case fails (100 vs 199) under the moved-term mutation and passes as written.

### nit — `tests/test_rules.c:400` duplicates a label already used at `tests/test_rules.c:431`

Both print `FAIL four kills earns it with a clean record`, so a failure in either does not say which precondition broke. Rename one, e.g. `"four kills earns it before any violation"`.

### nit — `tests/test_rules.c:387-405` splits a continuation

The new block lands between `"each penalty counted at its own rate"` and the comment that begins `/* And calls for help are worth forty-five apiece on their own. */`. The "And" no longer follows what it continues. Moving the CLOAKING block to the end of `test_promotion_penalties()`, after the starbase earned/not-earned pair it mirrors, reads better and puts the two structurally identical cases side by side.

## Answers to your four questions

**Placement and guard — correct.** `ncviol` is declared inside `#ifdef CLOAKING` in `sst.h:124` and `sst.h:223`, so the guard is not optional stylistic mirroring of `score_compute`, it is required to compile; I verified `rules.c` builds with `CLOAKING` undefined. The weight `100.0` matches `rules.c:57` and the score sheet line at `sst.doc:1374`, and the placement before the clamp is the right one (see the finding above for why it needs a test).

**Reachability and ordering — verified, and moot twice over.** `finish.c` `case FWON:` calls `promotion_compute` at line 98 and `score(0)` at line 154 and then `return`s, so it never reaches the shared tail where `case FCLOAK: ncviol++;` lives at line 284. Between those two lines only output, `chew()` and `ja()` run — none of them touch `ncviol`. Separately, `FCLOAK` is dead: its only trigger is commented out at `battle.c:63` (`// if (neutz && d.date >= ALGERON) finish(FCLOAK);`), so that increment cannot execute in the current build at all. The other four sites (`battle.c:59,89`, `sst.c:264,277`) are all inside the command loop and cannot run after `finish()` has been entered. The death penalty being moot is also verified: `promotion_compute` is called only inside `if (alive)` at `finish.c:93`.

**The reading — I agree with the code change, not a manual reword.** Three reasons beyond the plain text of `sst.doc:1383-1385`. (1) The rule as written is unqualified and points at a list the same page prints two paragraphs earlier; rewording the manual would mean inventing a distinction ("these six penalties, but not those two") that no version of the document has ever made and that has no in-fiction logic — a violated treaty is exactly the sort of thing Starfleet would weigh before a promotion. (2) The game already tells the player, on the very screen where promotion is announced, that the violation cost them 100 points (`finish.c:390-392`); a bar that ignores a penalty the score sheet itself just itemised is the inconsistency, not the rule. (3) The omission has the shape of age, not design — `promotion_compute`'s term list is exactly the pre-cloaking penalty set, and `score_compute` was updated for `ncviol` while this arithmetic, buried inline in `finish.c` until `bfe7726`, was not. Balance-wise the change introduces nothing new: one violation raises the Novice bar 0.3 → 1.1, identical to destroying one starbase, which the code has always done. (Unverified because I have no network here: my recollection is that ESR's modern `sst` includes `100*ncviol` in its `badpt` sum, which would be direct upstream corroboration — worth a glance if you have that tree handy, but the argument stands without it.)

**Evidence — the unit tests are acceptable, with the gap above closed.** The behaviour is reachable only through `FWON`, which requires clearing every Klingon in the galaxy; no scripted fixture is going to get there without a very lucky seed, and a golden recording of a won game would be a large, brittle artifact for this one line. I would not hold the slice for an end-to-end case. It is worth a separate issue, though: no golden fixture covers the `FWON` epilogue at all, so the promotion prose, the win bonus, and the citation prompt are entirely unrecorded — that is a gap wider than this change and should be its own slice rather than a rider on this one.

## Not reviewed

- Whether upstream `sst` counts `ncviol` in its promotion penalty (no network access) — noted above as unverified.
- The `tui` ctest target ran and passed on the default size only; I did not do the manual 80x24 / 72x24 pass, which is not relevant to a diff that changes no output path.

Failure scenario the current tests miss: 99 points of other penalty plus one violation. Correct behaviour is 199 (the violation carries the rest over the floor, and all of it counts). With the term after the clamp it is 100 — the ninety-nine silently vanish, and a captain who called for help twice and took nine casualties gets a bar 0.792 lower than the manual's rule gives them.

Suggested addition, next to the existing floor test:

```c
	/* Ninety-nine points is under the floor on its own; a violation
	   carries the rest of them over it, and then all of it counts. */
	nothing_happened();
	skill = SNOVICE;
	nhelp = 2;		/*  90 */
	casual = 9;		/*   9 */
	ncviol = 1;		/* 100 */
	promotion_compute(&p, 10.0);
	checkrate("a violation carries the rest over the floor",
		  p.penalties, 199.0);
```

I confirmed this case fails (100 vs 199) under the moved-term mutation and passes as written.

### nit — `tests/test_rules.c:400` duplicates a label already used at `tests/test_rules.c:431`

Both print `FAIL four kills earns it with a clean record`, so a failure in either does not say which precondition broke. Rename one, e.g. `"four kills earns it before any violation"`.

### nit — `tests/test_rules.c:387-405` splits a continuation

The new block lands between `"each penalty counted at its own rate"` and the comment that begins `/* And calls for help are worth forty-five apiece on their own. */`. The "And" no longer follows what it continues. Moving the CLOAKING block to the end of `test_promotion_penalties()`, after the starbase earned/not-earned pair it mirrors, reads better and puts the two structurally identical cases side by side.

## Answers to your four questions

**Placement and guard — correct.** `ncviol` is declared inside `#ifdef CLOAKING` in `sst.h:124` and `sst.h:223`, so the guard is not optional stylistic mirroring of `score_compute`, it is required to compile; I verified `rules.c` builds with `CLOAKING` undefined. The weight `100.0` matches `rules.c:57` and the score sheet line at `sst.doc:1374`, and the placement before the clamp is the right one (see the finding above for why it needs a test).

**Reachability and ordering — verified, and moot twice over.** `finish.c` `case FWON:` calls `promotion_compute` at line 98 and `score(0)` at line 154 and then `return`s, so it never reaches the shared tail where `case FCLOAK: ncviol++;` lives at line 284. Between those two lines only output, `chew()` and `ja()` run — none of them touch `ncviol`. Separately, `FCLOAK` is dead: its only trigger is commented out at `battle.c:63` (`// if (neutz && d.date >= ALGERON) finish(FCLOAK);`), so that increment cannot execute in the current build at all. The other four sites (`battle.c:59,89`, `sst.c:264,277`) are all inside the command loop and cannot run after `finish()` has been entered. The death penalty being moot is also verified: `promotion_compute` is called only inside `if (alive)` at `finish.c:93`.

**The reading — I agree with the code change, not a manual reword.** Three reasons beyond the plain text of `sst.doc:1383-1385`. (1) The rule as written is unqualified and points at a list the same page prints two paragraphs earlier; rewording the manual would mean inventing a distinction ("these six penalties, but not those two") that no version of the document has ever made and that has no in-fiction logic — a violated treaty is exactly the sort of thing Starfleet would weigh before a promotion. (2) The game already tells the player, on the very screen where promotion is announced, that the violation cost them 100 points (`finish.c:390-392`); a bar that ignores a penalty the score sheet itself just itemised is the inconsistency, not the rule. (3) The omission has the shape of age, not design — `promotion_compute`'s term list is exactly the pre-cloaking penalty set, and `score_compute` was updated for `ncviol` while this arithmetic, buried inline in `finish.c` until `bfe7726`, was not. Balance-wise the change introduces nothing new: one violation raises the Novice bar 0.3 → 1.1, identical to destroying one starbase, which the code has always done. (Unverified because I have no network here: my recollection is that ESR's modern `sst` includes `100*ncviol` in its `badpt` sum, which would be direct upstream corroboration — worth a glance if you have that tree handy, but the argument stands without it.)

**Evidence — the unit tests are acceptable, with the gap above closed.** The behaviour is reachable only through `FWON`, which requires clearing every Klingon in the galaxy; no scripted fixture is going to get there without a very lucky seed, and a golden recording of a won game would be a large, brittle artifact for this one line. I would not hold the slice for an end-to-end case. It is worth a separate issue, though: no golden fixture covers the `FWON` epilogue at all, so the promotion prose, the win bonus, and the citation prompt are entirely unrecorded — that is a gap wider than this change and should be its own slice rather than a rider on this one.

## Not reviewed

- Whether upstream `sst` counts `ncviol` in its promotion penalty (no network access) — noted above as unverified.
- The `tui` ctest target ran and passed on the default size only; I did not do the manual 80x24 / 72x24 pass, which is not relevant to a diff that changes no output path.

fix: let a broken treaty raise the promotion bar

Starfleet asks a higher kill rate of a captain who has lost a hundred
points or more in penalties. It counted six of the eight kinds the
score sheet lists. One of the two missing is the two hundred for
getting yourself killed, which cannot matter -- a dead captain is not
promoted. The other is the Treaty of Algeron, so a captain could cloak
in the Neutral Zone three times, watch the score sheet take three
hundred points off for it, and still be promoted on the rate a
spotless captain needs.

The manual states the rule without qualification and lists the
penalties two paragraphs earlier, so it is the code that was wrong.
The shape of the omission says the same thing: the term list is
exactly the pre-cloaking penalty set, and the score kept up with
cloaking while this did not.

Plain-mode output changes for a game that both breaks the treaty and
wins: one violation raises the novice bar from 0.3 to 1.1, which is
what destroying a starbase has always done.

No recording moved, and none could -- not one of them reaches a won
game, which is a wider gap than this change and is now #55. The tests
are the coverage: a violation is worth a hundred, a rate that earns
promotion stops earning it, and -- the part I could not see for myself
until review pointed at it -- the term is counted with the others
rather than after them. Ninety-nine points of anything else plus one
violation comes to a hundred and ninety-nine, not a hundred. Moving
the term below the floor passed the whole suite before that case
existed.

Fixes #53
