input.content:
Fixes #53.

Starfleet asks a higher kill rate of a captain who has lost a hundred
points or more in penalties. It counted **six of the eight kinds** the
score sheet lists.

One of the two missing is the 200 for getting yourself killed, which
cannot matter — a dead captain is not promoted. The other is the **Treaty
of Algeron**, so a captain could cloak in the Neutral Zone three times,
watch the score sheet take 300 points off for it on the very screen the
promotion is announced, and still be promoted on the rate a spotless
captain needs.

## Why the code and not the manual

The issue offered both routes. The manual states the rule without
qualification and lists the penalties two paragraphs earlier, so rewording
it would mean inventing a distinction — "these six, but not those two" —
that no version of the document has ever made.

The shape of the omission says the same thing: the term list is exactly
the pre-cloaking penalty set. Cloaking arrived behind `#ifdef CLOAKING`,
`score_compute()` was updated for it, and this arithmetic — buried inline
in `finish.c` until the previous slice pulled it out — was not.

Review reached the same conclusion independently and added a point I had
not: the game *already tells the player* on that screen that the violation
cost them 100 points, so a bar that ignores it is the inconsistency.

**Plain-mode output changes** for a game that both breaks the treaty and
wins: one violation raises the Novice bar from 0.3 to 1.1 — exactly what
destroying a starbase has always done, so nothing new enters the balance.

## Coverage

**No recording moved, and none could** — not one of the seven reaches a
won game. That is a wider gap than this change and is now #55.

So the unit tests are the coverage, and review found the one that
mattered missing. I asked whether the term's placement *before* the
100-point floor was right; it is, but nothing tested it. Moving it below
the floor passed the entire suite.

The case that now pins it: ninety-nine points of other penalty plus one
violation is **199, not 100** — the violation carries the rest over the
floor and then all of it counts. Both mutations (zeroing the term, moving
it past the floor) now fail.

Review also verified the ordering I claimed: `FWON` returns before the
shared tail where `case FCLOAK: ncviol++` lives, so nothing changes
`ncviol` between the promotion decision and the score — and noted that
`FCLOAK` is dead code anyway, its only trigger commented out at
`battle.c:63`.

10/10 ctest; zero warnings with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`; `golden.sh` and the
tournament battery unchanged; `rules.c` and the tests both still compile
with `CLOAKING` undefined.

content.text:
#53 is fixed and merged — `main` at `d0fdb93`, 10/10 green. (The first merge attempt hit a transient GitHub GraphQL error; the retry landed it.)

A broken treaty now raises the promotion bar. One violation takes the Novice bar from 0.3 to 1.1 — exactly what destroying a starbase has always done, so nothing new enters the balance.

**Why the code rather than the manual.** The rule is stated without qualification and points at a penalty list two paragraphs earlier; rewording would mean inventing a "these six, but not those two" distinction no version of the document has made. Review reached the same conclusion independently and added a point I'd missed: **the game already tells the player on that very screen that the violation cost them 100 points**, so a bar that ignores it is the inconsistency, not the rule.

**Review caught the test that mattered.** I asked specifically whether placing the term *before* the 100-point floor was right. It is — but nothing tested it, and moving it below the floor **passed the entire suite**. The case that pins it now: ninety-nine points of other penalty plus one violation is **199, not 100**. The violation carries the rest over the floor, and then all of it counts. Both mutations die now.

That's twice in two slices that the gap was in my tests rather than the code, and both times in the same place — a property I could see was true but hadn't asked anything to confirm.

Review also verified the ordering I'd claimed (`FWON` returns before the tail where `ncviol++` lives) and turned up that `FCLOAK` is dead code anyway, its only trigger commented out at `battle.c:63`.

**One gap I filed rather than papered over: [#55](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/55).** No golden recording reaches a won game — so the whole `FWON` epilogue is unrecorded: the promotion prose, the win bonus, the surrender line, the citation prompt. That's why `golden OK` said nothing about this change, and it means the recordings are weaker evidence than they look for anything near a game's end. Both of the last two slices got their confidence from differential harnesses run by hand, not from the suite. The issue weighs two routes — committing a near-won save to thaw, or a debug "win now" command.

**Remaining:** #55 (the win epilogue), #50 (more rule slices — impulse and shield energy costs next), #46 (resize repaint), #38 (`osx.c` declarations).

```c
ttime = (10.0*dist)/square(twarp);
tpower = dist*twarp*twarp*twarp*(shldup+1);
```

This is the ETA command — the one place a player is shown the warp cost as a *prediction* and can compare it against what the WARP command then charges. It is the highest-value remaining call site and it is a direct `warp_time(dist, twarp)` / `warp_energy(dist, twarp, shldup)` substitution. `reports.c` isn't in your diff; I'd pull it in rather than leave the branch's headline claim half-true.

`dist = power/(warpfac*warpfac*warpfac*(shldup+1));` is the inverse of `warp_energy` and expressible as `power/warp_energy(1.0, warpfac, shldup)`; `Time = 10.0*dist/wfacsq;` is `warp_time`. Lower stakes (emergency override), but they're the last two.

Either take `double shieldsup` to match the caller, or make the boolean intent explicit with `shieldsup ? 2 : 1` inside and a `!!` at the call site.

**7. nit — citation ranges**

`rules.c:103` cites `sst.doc:576-579` for a quote that begins at line 577 (576 is "depends on your current warp factor…"). `rules.h:57` says "626-627 for impulse" but the shields-up clause you rely on is on 628, which `rules.c:119` cites correctly. The file's own convention elsewhere (`sst.doc:1363-1365`) is exact, so these read as slips.

**8. Your judgement call on `test_shield_costs`: keep it.**

It is tautological as an assertion, but the manual restates both numbers a second time at `sst.doc:1464-1466` ("Shields cost 50 units of energy to raise… Engaging the high-speed shield control requires 200 units"), which makes the test a genuine two-source agreement rather than a mirror. Add that citation alongside 646/660 and the comment at `tests/test_rules.c:563-567` stops needing to apologise for itself.

**9. nit — `tests/test_rules.c:551-553` hand-rolls an absolute-difference check through `checkint`**

```c
checkint("impulse is about warp 0.975",
	 impulse_time(1.0) - warp_time(1.0, 0.975) < 0.05 && ... , 1);
```

On failure this prints `want: 1 / got: 0` and nothing about the two numbers that disagreed — which is exactly the diagnostic you'd want, given this assertion is (per finding 1) currently the only thing pinning `warp_time`'s coefficient. A `checkclose(what, got, want, tol)` helper next to `checkrate` would print both and read like the rest of the file.

---

### Not reviewed

- I did not exercise the TUI (`tests/tui.sh` ran green inside `ctest`; no tmux session of my own was created or destroyed).
- I verified behaviour preservation by reading the expressions rather than by differential execution; `golden.sh` passing is the empirical check, and it covers plain mode only.
- Mutation results above are mine, run against a scratch copy in the scratchpad; your worktree was not modified.

input.content:
Third slice of #50.

`sst.doc` states the movement rules outright in its appendix:

```
Shields cost 50 units of energy to raise, and double the power
    requirements of moving under warp drive.  Engaging the high-speed
    shield control requires 200 units of energy.
Warp drive requires (distance)*(warp factor cubed) units of energy
    to travel at a speed of (warp factor squared)/10 quadrants per stardate.
Impulse engines require 20 units to warm up, plus 100 units per
     quadrant.  Speed is just under one sector per stardate.
```

All of it was written out longhand wherever it was needed and nowhere it
could be asked about.

## The change

Four functions in `rules.c` — `warp_energy`, `warp_time`,
`impulse_energy`, `impulse_time` — and the two flat shield costs as named
constants that carry their citation to the call site instead of being a
bare `50.0` in the middle of `battle.c`.

**Nine call sites across four files** come to them, including the two a
player directly compares: the estimate the `computer` ETA command prints
and the charge the `warp` command makes were separate copies of the same
two formulas, in different files. A correction to one would have left the
other quoting the old rule — and the ETA is precisely where the player is
told what a jump will cost before deciding to make it.

## What the tests caught

Nothing in the game — the code agrees with the appendix everywhere. They
caught something in *me*.

My first draft asserted only **ratios**: warp 10 costs a thousand times
warp 1, warp 2 costs eight times, twice as far costs twice as much. My
stated reasoning was that the manual gives ratios and not a formula. That
was wrong — I had read the WARP FACTOR section and not the appendix,
which gives the closed form with its coefficient.

It cost a real assertion. Review demonstrated it: with ratios alone the
scale is free, and

```c
return 2.0*quadrants*factor*factor*factor*(shieldsup + 1);
```

— **doubling the price of every warp jump in the game** — passed the
entire suite. A quadrant at warp 1 costs one unit now, and takes ten
stardates, and those two assertions say so. Both mutations die.

## Smaller things review found

- Three bare `200` literals in `battle.c` were the *actual deductions*
  for the high-speed shield control, while what I had renamed were only
  the affordability checks and the display strings — backwards, and a

# Verdict: request changes

One should-fix (a one-line test addition). The refactor itself is behaviour-preserving and I found no defect in it.

**Reviewed state:** branch `test/rules-warp-damage-and-galaxy` at `2641970` (no commits ahead of `main`) plus the four-file unstaged working-tree diff — `rules.c` (blob `7197558`), `rules.h` (`80ab7fe`), `moving.c` (`e3f647a`), `tests/test_rules.c` (`5d93e78`). Nothing staged, no untracked files. I ran mutations against the tree and restored it; the hashes above are the post-restore state and match what I reviewed.

## Findings

### should-fix — the one boundary the rule turns on is untested; a mutant survives

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/test_rules.c:608-613`

The comment says "Ten stardates is where 'less than 10' stops applying", but the assertions bracket it at 9.0 and 11.0 and never touch 10.0. I mutated `rules.c:145` from `> 10.0` to `>= 10.0`, rebuilt, and `test_rules` printed "All tests passed". So the four-mutation check missed this one: the `WARP_INOPERATIVE` threshold — the single most consequential number in the new function, and the one you explicitly asked about — is not pinned by any test.

Fix: add one line to `test_warp_with_damaged_engines`, e.g.

```c
	checkint("ten stardates exactly is still warp 4",
		 warp_verdict(4.0, 10.0), WARP_OK);
```

On the substantive question: **`> 10.0` is the right reading and `>= 10.0` is not.** `sst.doc:572-573` says "damaged **less than** 10 stardates ... you can still go warp 4"; it states what holds strictly below 10 and is silent at exactly 10 and above. The manual therefore does not decide the boundary, so the tie-breaker is behaviour preservation, and the original `setwrp()`/`warp()` both used `> 10.0`. Keeping it is correct, but that makes it a code-derived decision sitting inside a doc-derived file — which is exactly the kind of thing that needs a test to hold it in place, and a half-sentence in the `rules.c` comment saying the manual is silent at exactly ten and the game's long-standing choice is to allow it.

Capping at exactly 4 (rather than "below 4") is unambiguously right: "you can still go warp 4" asserts warp 4 is reachable, and `warp_verdict(4.0, 5.0) == WARP_OK` pins it. That test already kills the `wanted >= 4.0` mutant.

### nit — `warp()` computes the same verdict twice

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/moving.c:532` and `:545`

Two calls with identical arguments, where `setwrp()` got a single call and a `switch`. It is correct today (nothing mutates `damage[DWARPEN]` between them), but it reads as if the second call might see something different, and it diverges from the shape you just established next door. A local `enum warpverdict v = warp_verdict(warpfac, damage[DWARPEN]);` above the two `if`s would fix both.

### nit — the `switch` cannot be checked by the compiler

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/moving.c:681-695`, `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/rules.h:94`

You asked whether a case can escape: no. **#50 is closed.** `main` at `be17114`, 10/10 green.

Every rule `sst.doc` states in numbers is now checked against it: the score's fifteen rules, the promotion threshold, warp energy and speed, impulse energy and speed, the two shield costs, and the engine-damage limits. All in `rules.c`, which computes and narrates nothing, with each expected value carrying the manual line it came from.

**The last slice's finding was the boundary I'd asked about and not tested.** "Damaged *less than* 10 stardates" says what holds below ten and nothing about exactly ten. The game has always allowed that one — so `> 10` versus `>= 10` is a decision, not a citation, and my four mutations had missed it. Review found `>= 10.0` passing the whole suite. The test now holds it and says in the file that this line records a choice rather than a quote.

That's four slices and four times the gap was the same shape: **the property I could see was true and hadn't asked anything to confirm.** Surrender and bonus never reaching the total; the Algeron term's position relative to the floor; the coefficient behind the exponents; now a boundary. Never the interesting part — always the part that looked too obvious to assert.

**I closed #50 on a corrected reason, not my original one.** I'd said galaxy invariants were blocked by `setup()`'s I/O. Review pointed out the stronger objection: **the invariant isn't in the manual.** The `d.galaxy` packing appears nowhere in `sst.doc`, so a test of it would take its expectations from the code and agree with the code by construction — exactly what `tests/test_rules.c` forbids in its own header. It'd be a consistency check wearing a second opinion's clothes. Filed **[#58](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/58)** for what *is* worth checking near it — the starbase count and grid dimensions, which the manual does state — as an end-to-end journey rather than a unit test.

**What the exercise bought, honestly:** one real defect (#53, the Treaty of Algeron not raising the promotion bar), and the rules pinned to their source with a seam for the next one. Six of the seven findings across four slices were in my tests, not the game. That's roughly what the issue predicted — a test written from a manual that already agrees with the code mostly proves the manual is usable — but the one it did find had survived thirty years and every other form of testing in the repo.

**Remaining:** #58, #55 (no recording reaches a won game), #46 (resize repaint), #38 (`osx.c` declarations).

## 1. Primary Request and Intent

The user drove a long sequence of work on **Super Star Trek** (C17/CMake terminal game at `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek`), in these explicit phases:

1. **Resume and land in-flight work** — retry the 1Password-blocked commit for the TUI colour work, then merge open PRs in order.
2. **Work issues in sequence**: #17 (first keystroke), #13 (TUI CI coverage), then #25 (briefing paging), #12 (seeded tournament journey), #14 (compiler warnings + `-Werror`).
3. **"Finish everything that is left to be done. You can merge the PRs when they are green. Don't stop until you are done. You can use a dynamic workflow to figure out how to do this. File PRs as you find things to address them later."** — autonomous clearing of the entire backlog.
4. **Strategic question**: "what should we focus on first to get the game in a good and verifiable state" → answered: portable seeded RNG, then golden masters.
5. **File an issue for unit-testing the game's rules**, then fix #42.
6. **Push back on my framing** of that issue ("Are you saying 50 is not worth the effort?"), then endorse the strong version: *"we should follow the strong... this is what would have happened if we dit this TDD"*.
7. **Execute #50 slice by slice**: score → promotion → fix #53 → movement/energy → "finish off 50".

**Standing process constraints (from AGENTS.md, must continue to apply):**
- Never commit directly to `main`; create a branch first.
- Run `ui-review` → `verifier` → `code-review` sub-agents before every commit; address all actionable findings; re-review if the reviewed state changes.
- Commits are SSH-signed via 1Password `op-ssh-sign`; **never bypass with `--no-gpgsign`** — retry, or hand the user a `! git commit -F <file>` command.
- Conventional Commits; commit trailer `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`; PR trailer `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.
- **tmux**: always `-L <unique-socket>` **and** `-f /dev/null`; never a bare `tmux kill-server`; never `kill-session` a session you did not create; never redirect the game's stdout in a tmux session. (A review agent once destroyed a week-old 8-pane session with a bare `kill-server`.)
- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect; deliberate changes must be stated and justified in the commit.
- A failing `golden` test must be explained in the commit — **never re-record with `--update` to turn CI green**.
- Merge only clean, green PRs; squash merge; delete the branch.

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **EXTERN/INCLUDED trick** in `sst.h`: exactly one TU per binary defines `INCLUDED` to instantiate ~90 globals. Display state (`tui_active`, `tui_ingame`) deliberately sits **outside** it — plain `extern` in `tui.h`, defined in `tui.c` — so `tui.h` is self-contained for `osx.c`.
- **`sst.h` `#define`s field accessors**: `dist`, `warpfac`, `Time`, `shldup` etc. expand to `a.dist` — so function *parameters* cannot use those names.
- **Pure-rule files**: `tuifmt.c` (panel formatters, curses-free) and now `rules.c`/`rules.h` (game rules, I/O-free). Both testable via `INCLUDED`-defining test binaries.
- **PCG-XSH-RR** portable PRNG replacing `rand()` so a tournament number names the same galaxy everywhere.
- **Golden-master / characterization testing** (`tests/golden.sh`) vs **spec-derived unit testing** (`tests/test_rules.c`).
- **Mutation testing** as the standard evidence that a test is non-vacuous.
- CRLF files: `sst.c`, `sst.h`, `setup.c`, `finish.c`, `battle.c`, `events.c`, `moving.c`, `reports.c`, `ai.c`, `planets.c`. LF: `tui.c`, `tuifmt.c`, `osx.c`, `rules.c`, `rules.h`, `tui.h`. Edits must preserve endings (use python, not sed).
- CI: 4 legs (ubuntu/macos × Debug/Release), `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, tmux installed on both.

## 3. Files and Code Sections

**`rules.h`** (new, LF) — declarations for pure rules. Contains `struct scoring`, `struct promotion`, the four movement functions, two shield constants, and `enum warpverdict`:
```c
enum warpverdict {
	WARP_OK,		/* the engines will do it */
	WARP_INOPERATIVE,	/* too damaged to run at all */
	WARP_LIMITED,		/* damaged: warp 4 is the most on offer */
	WARP_TOO_FAST,		/* above the ship's top speed */
	WARP_TOO_SLOW		/* below the bottom of the range */
};
int warp_verdict(double wanted, double enginedamage);

double warp_energy(double quadrants, double factor, double shieldsup);
double warp_time(double quadrants, double factor);
double impulse_energy(double quadrants);
double impulse_time(double quadrants);
#define SHIELD_RAISE_COST	(50.0)
#define FAST_SHIELD_COST	(200.0)
```
Parameter names are `quadrants`/`factor` because `sst.h` turns `dist`/`warpfac` into struct members.

**`rules.c`** (new, LF) — `score_compute()`, `promotion_compute()`, the four movement formulas, and:
```c
int warp_verdict(double wanted, double enginedamage)
{
	/* "If warp engines are damaged less than 10 stardates (undocked)
	   you can still go warp 4." -- sst.doc:572-573. ...
	   Two things the sentence leaves open. It says what holds below
	   ten and nothing about a ship damaged exactly ten: the game has
	   always allowed that one, so this does too... And "(undocked)"
	   describes no condition here -- docking divides the repair time
	   and never lifts the cap... */
	if (enginedamage > 10.0) return WARP_INOPERATIVE;
	if (enginedamage > 0.0 && wanted > 4.0) return WARP_LIMITED;
	if (wanted > 10.0) return WARP_TOO_FAST;
	if (wanted < 1.0) return WARP_TOO_SLOW;
	return WARP_OK;
}
```
Movement formulas cite `sst.doc:1467-1468` (the appendix closed form) as primary.

**`moving.c`** — `setwrp()`'s four `if` blocks became a `switch (warp_verdict(aaitem, damage[DWARPEN]))` with `default: break;` falling through to the assignment. `warp()` hoists one call:
```c
verdict = warp_verdict(warpfac, damage[DWARPEN]);
if (verdict == WARP_INOPERATIVE) { ... }
if (verdict == WARP_LIMITED) { ... }
```
Also: `warp_energy`/`warp_time`/`impulse_energy`/`impulse_time` at 5+ call sites, including `atover`'s inverse `dist = power/warp_energy(1.0, warpfac, shldup);`.

```c
	checkint("nine stardates of damage still gives warp 4",
		 warp_verdict(4.0, 9.0), WARP_OK);
	checkint("ten exactly still gives warp 4",
		 warp_verdict(4.0, 10.0), WARP_OK);
```

**`tests/tournament.sh`** — 12 chosen seeds `"7 4 12 6 16 9 19 20 11 21 1 23"`, two alternating routes (position selects route), per-journey + battery-wide assertions.

**`tests/tui.sh`** — tmux pty test; `tm() { tmux -f /dev/null -L "$socket" "$@"; }`; all grep helpers use `--`.

**`sst.doc`** — the oracle. Key citations used: 1352-1378 (score), 1380-1387 (promotion), 572-573 (warp damage), 598-599 (warp range/ratios), 1467-1468 (warp closed forms), 626-628/1469-1470 (impulse), 646/660/1464-1466 (shields), 1456 (distances in quadrants).

Closes #50.

`sst.doc:572-573` says a ship whose warp drive is damaged less than ten
stardates can still make warp 4; `sst.doc:598` says the factor runs from
1 to 10. Both were written out **twice** — once where the player sets the
factor and once where they try to move at it, because the engines can
take damage in between. Two copies of a rule that must agree.

One now, in `rules.c`, answering with a verdict the two callers act on.
`setwrp()`'s four sequential `if` blocks become a `switch`; `warp()` uses
two of the five verdicts.

## The boundary the manual does not give

The tests ask the manual for the four thresholds — and one of them is not
the manual's to give. "Damaged **less than** 10 stardates" says what holds
below ten and nothing about a ship damaged *exactly* ten.

The game has always let that one make warp 4, so the test holds it there,
and says in as many words that the line records a decision rather than a
citation. Without it `> 10` and `>= 10` are the same file.

**Review demonstrated that** — my own four mutations had missed exactly
that boundary, which is the one I had explicitly asked about. Fourth
slice, fourth time the gap was the property I could see was true and
hadn't asked anything to confirm.

`(undocked)` in the quoted sentence describes nothing here: docking
divides the repair time and never lifts the cap. Said so, rather than
letting the qualifier vanish between the quote and the code.

## Closing #50

This finishes the rules `sst.doc` states in numbers: the score, the
promotion threshold, warp and impulse energy and speed, the shield costs,
and now the engine-damage limits.

What #50 listed and this does not do is the galaxy invariants — and the
reason is not the I/O obstacle I first gave. **The invariant is not in the
manual.** The packing of `d.galaxy` appears nowhere in `sst.doc`, so a
test of it would take its expectations from the code and agree with the
code by construction, which is the one thing `tests/test_rules.c` forbids
at the top of the file. `golden.sh` already answers "did the encoding
change" more cheaply.

#58 carries what *is* worth checking near it — the starbase count and the
grid dimensions, which the manual does state — and puts it in an
end-to-end journey rather than a unit test.

`golden.sh` unchanged; 10/10 ctest; zero warnings with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`;
five mutations of the thresholds each fail the matching test.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Third slice of #50.

`sst.doc` states the movement rules outright in its appendix:

```
Shields cost 50 units of energy to raise, and double the power
    requirements of moving under warp drive.  Engaging the high-speed
    shield control requires 200 units of energy.
Warp drive requires (distance)*(warp factor cubed) units of energy
    to travel at a speed of (warp factor squared)/10 quadrants per stardate.
Impulse engines require 20 units to warm up, plus 100 units per
     quadrant.  Speed is just under one sector per stardate.
```

All of it was written out longhand wherever it was needed and nowhere it
could be asked about.

## The change

Four functions in `rules.c` — `warp_energy`, `warp_time`,
`impulse_energy`, `impulse_time` — and the two flat shield costs as named
constants that carry their citation to the call site instead of being a
bare `50.0` in the middle of `battle.c`.

**Nine call sites across four files** come to them, including the two a
player directly compares: the estimate the `computer` ETA command prints
and the charge the `warp` command makes were separate copies of the same
two formulas, in different files. A correction to one would have left the
other quoting the old rule — and the ETA is precisely where the player is
told what a jump will cost before deciding to make it.

## What the tests caught

Nothing in the game — the code agrees with the appendix everywhere. They
caught something in *me*.

My first draft asserted only **ratios**: warp 10 costs a thousand times
warp 1, warp 2 costs eight times, twice as far costs twice as much. My
stated reasoning was that the manual gives ratios and not a formula. That
was wrong — I had read the WARP FACTOR section and not the appendix,
which gives the closed form with its coefficient.

It cost a real assertion. Review demonstrated it: with ratios alone the
scale is free, and

```c
return 2.0*quadrants*factor*factor*factor*(shieldsup + 1);
```

— **doubling the price of every warp jump in the game** — passed the
entire suite. A quadrant at warp 1 costs one unit now, and takes ten
stardates, and those two assertions say so. Both mutations die.

## Smaller things review found

- Three bare `200` literals in `battle.c` were the *actual deductions*
  for the high-speed shield control, while what I had renamed were only
  the affordability checks and the display strings — backwards, and a
  change to the constant would have charged one number and checked
  against another.
- `moving.c`'s pre-flight time estimate was the last inline copy of
  `warp_time`, thirty lines from the charge that now goes through it.
- `warp_energy` took `int shieldsup` while every caller passes the
  `double shldup` — a silent narrowing `-Wall -Wextra` does not
  diagnose. Now `double`, with the boolean intent explicit.
- The near-equivalence check for "impulse is about warp 0.975" was
  hand-rolled through `checkint` and printed `want: 1 / got: 0` on
  failure. There is a `checkclose` helper now.

Two parameters are called `quadrants` and `factor` rather than `dist` and
`warpfac` because `sst.h` turns both of those names into struct members —
a parameter called `dist` expands to `a.dist` and does not compile.

`golden.sh` unchanged; 10/10 ctest; zero warnings with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`.

Fixes #53.

Starfleet asks a higher kill rate of a captain who has lost a hundred
points or more in penalties. It counted **six of the eight kinds** the
score sheet lists.

One of the two missing is the 200 for getting yourself killed, which
cannot matter — a dead captain is not promoted. The other is the **Treaty
of Algeron**, so a captain could cloak in the Neutral Zone three times,
watch the score sheet take 300 points off for it on the very screen the
promotion is announced, and still be promoted on the rate a spotless
captain needs.

## Why the code and not the manual

The issue offered both routes. The manual states the rule without
qualification and lists the penalties two paragraphs earlier, so rewording
it would mean inventing a distinction — "these six, but not those two" —
that no version of the document has ever made.

The shape of the omission says the same thing: the term list is exactly
the pre-cloaking penalty set. Cloaking arrived behind `#ifdef CLOAKING`,
`score_compute()` was updated for it, and this arithmetic — buried inline
in `finish.c` until the previous slice pulled it out — was not.

Review reached the same conclusion independently and added a point I had
not: the game *already tells the player* on that screen that the violation
cost them 100 points, so a bar that ignores it is the inconsistency.

**Plain-mode output changes** for a game that both breaks the treaty and
wins: one violation raises the Novice bar from 0.3 to 1.1 — exactly what
destroying a starbase has always done, so nothing new enters the balance.

## Coverage

**No recording moved, and none could** — not one of the seven reaches a
won game. That is a wider gap than this change and is now #55.

So the unit tests are the coverage, and review found the one that
mattered missing. I asked whether the term's placement *before* the
100-point floor was right; it is, but nothing tested it. Moving it below
the floor passed the entire suite.

The case that now pins it: ninety-nine points of other penalty plus one
violation is **199, not 100** — the violation carries the rest over the
floor and then all of it counts. Both mutations (zeroing the term, moving
it past the floor) now fail.

Review also verified the ordering I claimed: `FWON` returns before the
shared tail where `case FCLOAK: ncviol++` lives, so nothing changes
`ncviol` between the promotion decision and the score — and noted that
`FCLOAK` is dead code anyway, its only trigger commented out at
`battle.c:63`.

10/10 ctest; zero warnings with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`; `golden.sh` and the
tournament battery unchanged; `rules.c` and the tests both still compile
with `CLOAKING` undefined.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- claude-security:claude-security: The dedicated Claude Security orchestrator. Hand it an unattended job — "fully scan this repository and patch what you find; I understand it will use a lot of tokens" — and it runs the whole thing itself: capturing the revision, driving the multi-agent scan through the claude-security:scan workflow, assembling the verified report, and turning survivors into targeted patch files you apply when you choose, each verified by a panel of agents before it is written. Best as the main agent of a session. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Write, Edit, AskUserQuestion, Workflow, Workflow(claude-security:scan), TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent(claude-security:scan-inventory, claude-security:scan-researcher, claude-security:scan-verifier, claude-security:patch-generator, claude-security:patch-verifier, claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:explore: Read-only code explorer that the plugin's other agents dispatch to map a codebase — locate files, trace how a flow is wired, find every caller of a symbol, answer "where does X happen". (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)

- claude-security:patch-generator: Implements the fix for one finding inside a scratch workspace clone, staged for review and delivery as a patch file; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Edit, Write, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:patch-verifier: The single verifier per fix round — reviews the workspace's staged diff against the finding, runs the tests, and states the three confidence claims a patch file must earn; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:scan-inventory: Restricted read-only repository cartographer dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to partition the tree into components and account for every top-level directory; not for direct invocation or vulnerability research. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- claude-security:scan-researcher: Restricted read-only vulnerability researcher dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow; not for direct invocation or general exploration. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:scan-verifier: Restricted read-only verifier dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to vote on one candidate finding; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- code-review: Expert code review of the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and untracked file. Invoke before every commit, and again after any change to the reviewed state. Read-only — reports findings and an explicit approve/request-changes verdict, never edits files. (Tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-review: Reviews the user-facing behavior of the Super Star Trek CLI game after an implementation pass. Acts as an expert in games and CLI games. Invoke after the main agent completes an implementation pass and before running the verifier. Read-only — reports findings, never edits files. (Tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob)

- verifier: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the current change. Invoke after ui-review and before code-review, and rerun after any code change made in response to a finding. Read-only — reports findings, never fixes them. (Tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob)

content.text:
Say `/clear`, then in the fresh session:

> Let's do #46.

That's genuinely enough. Substitute whichever issue you want — #58, #55, #46, or #38.

**Why so little works here:** everything a new session needs is already on disk or on GitHub.

- `AGENTS.md` loads automatically and carries the whole workflow — branch first, ui-review → verifier → code-review, tmux rules, Conventional Commits.
- `gh issue view 46` has the problem statement.
- `git log` has the reasoning behind every slice, since the commit messages say why and not just what.
- `tests/test_rules.c` states in its own header why expectations come from `sst.doc` and never from running the code.

That was the point of writing it down as we went. A fresh session re-reads it instead of me summarizing it.

**Two things aren't written down anywhere**, and you may want to paste them if they come up:

1. `AGENTS.md` documents `tmux -L <socket>` but not `-f /dev/null` — which we added after a stray user config interfered with a capture. Worth a one-line PR to that file if you'd like it permanent; say the word and I'll do it before you clear.
2. #46 (resize) was deliberately scoped out of the earlier TUI work because every repaint arrangement I tried blanked the screen, and `main` behaves the same way. So it's a known-hard one, not a quick fix — expect to spend real time in `tui.c`. The issue says this, but not how many arrangements failed.

If you'd rather not think about which issue: **#38 is the good-first-issue** (`osx.c` declares `min`, `max`, and `getch` where the compiler can't check them) and **#55 is the highest value** — no golden recording reaches a won game, which is why the Algeron fix in #53 had no end-to-end coverage and had to lean entirely on unit tests.
